text:
LiteRT-LM has its own Message and Content classes. _mk_content turns a string, bytes or a Path into the right content type, telling image from audio by the bytes themselves or by the file extension. _mk_msg and _mk_msgs build whole messages from those.

import tempfile
from fastcore.test import test_eq, test_fail


test_eq(_mk_msg("hello").to_json(), {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "hello"}]})
test_eq(_mk_msg("hi", role="model").to_json()["role"], Role.MODEL.value)
test_eq(_mk_msg("hi", role="assistant").role, Role.MODEL)   # either spelling, whichever litert-lm names it
test_eq([x["role"] for x in _mk_msgs(["a", _mk_msg("b", role="model")])], ["user", Role.MODEL.value])
assert isinstance(_mk_content("x"), Text)
# bytes are sniffed: image vs audio
assert isinstance(_mk_content(b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + b'\x00'*16), ImageBytes)
assert isinstance(_mk_content(b'RIFF\x00\x00\x00\x00WAVE' + b'\x00'*16), AudioBytes)

title: litert
text:
Portable history
rishi’s history is a list of OpenAI-shaped dicts, while LiteRT-LM speaks its own Message objects and calls the assistant model. fmt2hist converts LiteRT-LM messages into history dicts, and hist2fmt converts them back. That is what lets a conversation started here continue on llama.cpp or a hosted model through messages=, and the reverse. Images and audio from earlier turns become [image] and [audio] placeholders on the way into the history.

title: litert
text:
LiteRT callbacks
Urai’s chats run callbacks at fixed points in a turn. LiteRT-LM needs its own versions of three of them, because the engine keeps the conversation itself. _HistoryCallback copies each message and reply into chat.hist in the shared format. _UsageCallback works out token usage from how much the conversation’s token_count grew during the turn. _ToolReminderCallback appends a short reminder of the available tools to the outgoing message.

title: litert
text:
Tool calling
LiteRT-LM runs the tool loop inside the engine. The other local backends run it in rishi. The engine calls your Python function and feeds the result back to the model. ChatToolHandler connects that loop to the chat. Before each call it runs the chat’s before_tool_calls callbacks, checks the tool-call budget, and asks the chat’s approve function if there is one. A refused call is recorded with its reason instead of running. The handler writes each call and its result into chat.hist, and runs the after_tool_calls callbacks after each result. Approval itself is described on Urai’s chat page.
Several chats can share one engine. The engine runs one generation at a time. engine_lock returns the single lock of an engine, and a chat holds it for the length of a turn. The chat releases it while a tool runs, and the tool can use the engine. Chats on other threads wait their turn. A second chat on the same thread cannot wait, because the thread that holds the lock would never release it. That chat raises EngineBusy at once.
EngineHold is that hold for one send. Use it as a context manager, or call take and let_go. ChatToolHandler calls let_go while a tool runs and take after it. A chat that already holds the engine on this thread can take it again. recover_context and a one-shot call from a callback do this. The lock is a plain Lock, so closing a stream abandoned on another thread frees the engine. The old name _Hold still works.

title: litert
text:
Loading models and LitertChat
A .litertlm repo may hold several builds: a portable one, and others made for one kind of hardware, whose names contain -gpu, -npu, -web or an underscore. get_model prefers the portable build. Searches of the repository exclude file names that contain web. An existing model_path bypasses that filter. It finds the file in three steps. It uses a model_path you pass if the file exists. Otherwise it uses a portable build in the local Hugging Face cache. Otherwise it downloads a build, and uses a hardware-specific cached build only when the repo has no portable build or the Hub is unreachable. It raises FileNotFoundError when neither the cache nor the repo has a .litertlm file. cached_model is the cache step on its own. It returns the cached path, or None, without using the network. The old names _get_model and _cached_model still work.
LitertChat.create_engine builds the engine. Unless you name a backend, it tries the GPU first and falls back to the CPU with a warning. Set RISHI_LITERT_GPU=0 to skip the GPU attempt. Pass backend=Backend.GPU() or backend=Backend.CPU() to choose the hardware. On the GPU, activations default to 32-bit floats. With multimodal=True, the default, it also builds the vision and audio encoders that the model file contains. vision_backend and audio_backend choose their hardware, CPU by default. A backend named for an encoder the file lacks gives a warning. cache_dir is the LiteRT-LM cache directory. rishi creates it if it is missing.
think=True turns thinking on. filter_think, on by default, keeps the thought tokens out of the key-value cache (KV cache), where LiteRT-LM stores the keys and values computed for earlier tokens. constrain switches on constrained decoding, which keeps tool calls well formed. It defaults to on when the chat has tools. parallel_tools=True raises NotImplementedError, because the engine’s loop runs one call at a time. If the context window fills during a turn, the chat drops messages from the middle of the history, rebuilds the conversation and sends the turn again. It keeps the first 2 and the last 6 messages. It raises ContextWindowExceededError when nothing can be dropped.
The constants below are the Gemma 4 builds from litert-community.

title: litert
text:
Recorded model behaviour
These checks run against replies recorded from the real gemma4_e2b model. Urai’s CachedChat replays a recorded reply when it sees the same request again, without loading the model. Each check opens a fresh CachedChat, and they work on a temporary copy of nbs/chatcache so the recordings stay unchanged. They cover one turn, a second turn, a changed system prompt, a one-shot call, a prompt too long for the context window, and a tool call that LiteRT-LM ran itself.

# A normal turn records the response and canonical history produced by LiteRT.
c = CachedChat(**_litert_record_kw)
r = c('Reply with exactly: pong')
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'pong')
test_eq(c.hist, [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Reply with exactly: pong'},
                 {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'pong'}])
c.close()


# A second turn sees the first through LiteRT's conversation history.
c = CachedChat(**_litert_record_kw)
c('Reply with exactly: pong')
r = c('What exact word did you just reply with? Reply with only that word.')
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'pong')
test_eq([m['role'] for m in c.hist], ['user', 'assistant', 'user', 'assistant'])
c.close()


# Reconfiguration reaches the model without retaining state from another check.
c = CachedChat(**_litert_record_kw)
c.reconfigure(sp='Reply with exactly the word anchor, whatever the user asks.')
r = c('What is two plus two?')
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'anchor')
c.close()


# One-shots use a throwaway LiteRT conversation and do not change history.
c = CachedChat(**_litert_record_kw)
test_eq(c.oneshot('Reply with exactly: solo', think=False, max_tokens=16), 'solo')
test_eq(c.hist, [])
c.close()


c = CachedChat(**{**_litert_record_kw, 'ctx': 64})
test_fail(lambda: c.oneshot('x '*200, think=False, max_tokens=16),
          contains='201 tokens, over the 64-token context window')
test_eq(c.hist, [])
c.close()


# Tool history comes from a real native LiteRT tool round.
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    "Add two integers."
    return a + b

c = CachedChat(**_litert_record_kw, tools=[add])
r = c('Use the add tool to add 2 and 3. Reply with only the result.')
test_eq(resp_text(c.hist[1]), '')
test_eq(c.hist[1]['tool_calls'][0]['function']['name'], 'add')
test_eq(c.hist[2]['role'], 'tool')
test_eq(c.hist[2]['content'], '5.0')
assert '5' in resp_text(r)
c.close()


# fmt2hist / hist2fmt round-trip (model-free)
_nat = [
    'hi',
    Message.model(Contents.of('hello')).to_json(),
    {'role': 'model', 'tool_calls': [{'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}}}]},
    {'role': 'tool', 'content': [{'type': 'tool_response', 'name': 'add', 'response': 5}]},
]
_canon = LitertChat.fmt2hist(_nat)
test_eq(_canon[0], {'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'})
test_eq(_canon[1], {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'hello'})
test_eq(_canon[2]['role'], 'assistant')
test_eq(_canon[2]['tool_calls'][0]['function'], {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}})
assert _canon[2]['tool_calls'][0]['id']                       # a synthetic id was assigned
test_eq(_canon[3], {'role': 'tool', 'name': 'add', 'content': '5'})

# canonical -> litert Messages ready for the engine
_ms = LitertChat.hist2fmt(_canon)
test_eq([m.role for m in _ms], [Role.USER, Role.MODEL, Role.MODEL, Role.TOOL])
test_eq(str(_ms[1]), 'hello')
test_eq(_ms[2].tool_calls[0].name, 'add')
test_eq(_ms[3].contents.to_json(), [{'type': 'tool_response', 'name': 'add', 'response': '5'}])

# fmt2hist is idempotent on an already-canonical (llama-origin) tool round
_llama = [{'role': 'assistant', 'content': '', 'tool_calls': [{'id': 'call_x', 'type': 'function',
                                                               'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 1}}}]},
          {'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'call_x', 'name': 'add', 'content': '1'}]
test_eq(LitertChat.fmt2hist(_llama), _llama)


class _FakeCtx:
    ctx_limit = 100
    def count_tokens(self, text): return len(text)
_f = _FakeCtx()
LitertChat._ck_fits(_f, 'x'*100)
test_fail(lambda: LitertChat._ck_fits(_f, 'x'*101), contains='101 tokens')
test_fail(lambda: LitertChat._ck_fits(_f, 'x'*61, sp='y'*40), contains='over the 100-token')
_f.ctx_limit = None
LitertChat._ck_fits(_f, 'x'*10000)

When the window fills after a tool round, the rebuilt conversation keeps only history from before the turn and the turn message is sent again. A stream closed early cancels the native generation.

# Chats sharing one engine take turns on it (model-free)
import time
from types import SimpleNamespace
def _free(lock):
    "Whether another thread could take `lock` right now."
    out = []
    def _try():
        ok = lock.acquire(blocking=False); out.append(ok)
        if ok: lock.release()
    t = threading.Thread(target=_try); t.start(); t.join()
    return out[0]
def _chat(eng, **kw): return SimpleNamespace(engine=eng, cbs=L(), _budget_exceeded=False, max_steps=None, _steps=0, approve=None, hist=[], tool_max_len=None, **kw)
_eng = SimpleNamespace(); _lk = engine_lock(_eng)
assert engine_lock(_eng) is _lk and _free(_lk)

# Two threads: sends never overlap
_log = []
def _send(ch, tag):
    with EngineHold(ch): _log.append((tag, 'in')); time.sleep(0.05); _log.append((tag, 'out'))
_ts = [threading.Thread(target=_send, args=(_chat(_eng), t)) for t in 'ab']
for t in _ts: t.start()
for t in _ts: t.join()
test_eq([x[1] for x in _log], ['in', 'out', 'in', 'out'])
assert _free(_lk)

# One thread, two streams: the second fails fast instead of hanging the thread that holds the first
def _stream(ch):
    with EngineHold(ch): yield 1; yield 2
_c1, _c2 = _chat(_eng), _chat(_eng)
_a = _stream(_c1); next(_a)
_b = _stream(_c2)
test_fail(lambda: next(_b), contains='mid-turn on this engine')
_a.close(); assert _free(_lk)
test_eq(list(_stream(_c2)), [1, 2]); assert _free(_lk)   # `_b` died with the error; a fresh stream gets in

# A stream abandoned on another thread frees the engine when closed from this one
_box = []
_t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: (_box.append(_stream(_chat(_eng))), next(_box[0]))); _t.start(); _t.join()
assert not _free(_lk)
_box[0].close(); assert _free(_lk)

# An exception mid-stream lets go
def _bad(ch):
    with EngineHold(ch): yield 1; raise ValueError('boom')
_g = _bad(_c1); next(_g); test_fail(lambda: next(_g), contains='boom'); assert _free(_lk)

# The same chat, deeper in its own turn (recover_context, a one-shot from a callback), gets straight in
with EngineHold(_c1):
    with EngineHold(_c1): assert not _free(_lk)
    assert not _free(_lk)
assert _free(_lk)

# The tool loop lets go while a tool runs, so a tool may use the engine, and takes it back for the reply
_ch = _chat(_eng); _ch._hold, _th = EngineHold(_ch), ChatToolHandler(_ch)
with _ch._hold:
    assert not _free(_lk)
    assert _th.approve_tool_call({'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}}})
    assert _free(_lk)
    with EngineHold(_c2): pass                       # another chat on this thread, from inside the tool
    test_eq(_th.process_tool_response('5'), '5')
    assert not _free(_lk)
assert _free(_lk)
test_eq([m['role'] for m in _ch.hist], ['assistant', 'tool'])
_ch._hold.let_go(); assert _free(_lk)           # letting go twice is harmless

Utilities and bench
classify, structured and check come from Urai and work here as on every backend. The example below classifies a sentence and extracts a dataclass from another. bench() is particular to LiteRT-LM. It runs LiteRT-LM’s Benchmark on a model and reports the load time, the time to the first token, and the prefill and decode speeds in tokens per second. It uses the CPU backend and 64 prefill and 64 decode tokens unless you pass backend, prefill_tokens or decode_tokens. This backend has no log-likelihood scoring. LiteRT-LM cannot score how likely a given text is.

title: litert
text:
Sharing one engine
A LiteRT-LM Engine lives inside one process, so separate programs cannot attach to it. LitertBroker keeps one in a long-lived process and serves a LitertChat to each client over a Unix socket. Each client has its own conversation and history, and all of them share one copy of the weights. Turns run one at a time, because one engine cannot be driven from two threads at once. The protocol is Urai’s ChatBroker, described on Urai’s broker page.


source

LitertBroker
def LitertBroker(
    address, engine:NoneType=None, model_id:str='litert-community/gemma-4-E2B-it-litert-lm', **engine_kw
):
Serve one LiteRT-LM engine to several processes over a Unix socket, each client with its own LitertChat conversation.

title: rishi
text:
rishi lets you use a language model from Python with the same calls, whether the model runs on your machine or on a remote server. Each way of running a model is a backend. Four backends run models locally: LiteRT-LM, llama.cpp, MLX and Ollama. Three backends send the conversation to another program or server: a hosted API such as OpenAI or Anthropic, your Claude Code installation, and GitHub Copilot. Each of these seven has its own message format and its own way to pass images and tool calls.
rishi uses one conversation format for all of them. The conversation is called the history. The history is a Python list of message dicts in the OpenAI format, such as {'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'}. It is stored in chat.hist. Every backend reads and writes that list. You can start a conversation on a small local model, give the list to a hosted model, and the hosted model continues the conversation.
The parts that all backends share come from Urai, which is published on PyPI as uraiyadal. These are the Chat class, tool calling, streaming, options and recorded replies. rishi adds the seven backends and registers them with Urai. from rishi import * gives you the names from Urai and from rishi.

title: rishi
text:
Install
The base package includes LiteRT-LM and the three backends that send the conversation to another program or server. The other local backends need optional extras. Install only the extras you use:
pip install rishi                # LiteRT-LM, hosted APIs, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot
pip install 'rishi[llama]'       # llama.cpp, for GGUF model files
pip install 'rishi[mlx]'         # MLX, on Apple Silicon Macs
pip install 'rishi[mlx-vlm]'     # MLX vision and audio models
pip install 'rishi[ollama]'      # Ollama; on Linux before Python 3.14 this also installs zstandard
pip install 'rishi[all]'         # every extra above
You can combine extras, as in rishi[llama,mlx]. rishi imports a backend module only when a chat first needs it. A missing extra causes no error until you ask for that backend. The hosted backends use their usual credentials. Hosted APIs need an API key in the environment. Claude Code needs a signed-in claude command. Copilot needs a GitHub sign-in.

title: rishi
text:
Chat
Chat(model) opens one conversation. The model name selects the backend. rishi recognizes a .litertlm build, a -GGUF repo, an mlx-community repo, an Ollama hf.co/ id, and a hosted name such as gpt-5.1. A prefix such as claude/ or copilot/ selects the backend directly. With no model, Chat uses LiteRT-LM and its default model, Gemma 4 E2B. The core page lists the exact rules.
Call the chat with a prompt to send one turn. The call returns the reply, a dict that Urai calls a Resp. Each call appends the prompt and the reply to chat.hist. The second question below is therefore asked with the first exchange in the history. resp_text returns the answer text from a reply. close() frees the model memory.

chat = Chat(gemma4_e2b)
print(resp_text(chat('Give one fact about lobsters.')))
print(resp_text(chat('Give one more.')))
chat.close()

Lobsters are crustaceans, which means they have a hard exoskeleton and eight legs.
Lobsters are known for their ability to change their color and texture to blend in with their surroundings, a behavior called camouflage.

title: rishi
text:
Streaming
Pass stream=True to receive a reply as it is generated. The call then returns an iterator of markdown strings instead of one reply. Urai renders the events of every backend into the same markdown. Thinking and tool calls look the same on every backend. Pass stream='raw' to receive the chunk dicts that the markdown is built from.

chat = Chat(gemma4_e2b)
for markdown in chat('Write a two-line poem about rain.', stream=True):
    print(markdown, end='', flush=True)
chat.close()

Soft drops tap on the pane,
Washing the world clean again.

title: rishi
text:
Images
To ask about a picture, pass a list instead of a string. The list holds the prompt text and the image. The image can be a Path, raw bytes or a PIL.Image. Every backend that accepts images accepts the same list. The model must accept image input. Gemma 4 on LiteRT-LM does. The page of each backend names other models.

chat = Chat(gemma4_e2b)
image = repo_root()/'nbs/images.jpeg'
display(Image.open(image))
print(resp_text(chat(['Describe this image in one sentence.', image])))
chat.close()








A medium-sized, reddish-brown German Shepherd is looking attentively off to the side with its mouth slightly open.

title: rishi
text:
Audio
Pass audio in the same list as the prompt, as a file path or as bytes. The model needs an audio encoder. Gemma 4 on LiteRT-LM has one. Some llama.cpp and MLX models have one. Claude Code, Ollama and text-only models raise an error. They do not drop the clip.

chat = Chat(gemma4_e2b)
audio = repo_root()/'nbs/speech.wav'
print(resp_text(chat(['Transcribe this clip.', audio])))
chat.close()

Dancing in the masquerade, idol truth in plain sight jaded, pop, roll, click, dot, who will I be today or not? But such a tide as moving seems asleep, too full for sound and foam, when that drew from out the boundless deep turns again home, twilight and evening bell and after that.

title: rishi
text:
One conversation across seven backends
Every backend uses the same history format. A conversation can move between backends. The example below has seven legs. Each leg opens a new Chat with messages=history, sends one prompt, and passes the longer history to the next leg. The first leg uses Gemma on LiteRT-LM. Its prompt gives the code word “amber”. The next six legs use Qwen3 on Ollama, Qwen3 on MLX, Qwen3 on llama.cpp, GPT-4.1 through the hosted API, Claude Haiku through Claude Code, and GPT-4.1 through Copilot. Each of them is asked for the code word and answers “amber”. It can know this only from the history.
The example downloads four local models. The last three legs need their credentials.

legs = [
    ('LiteRT', gemma4_e2b, {}),
    ('Ollama', f'ollama/{ollama_qwen}', {'think': True}),
    ('MLX', mlx_qwen, {}),
    ('llama.cpp', llama_qwen, {'n_ctx': 4096}),
    ('cloud', 'gpt-4.1', {}),
    ('Claude', 'claude/haiku', {}),
    ('Copilot', 'copilot/gpt-4.1', {}),
]

history = []
for i, (name, model, options) in enumerate(legs):
    chat = Chat(model, messages=history, **options)
    prompt = (
        'The code word is amber. Start a travel log with one short sentence.'
        if i == 0 else
        f'What is the code word? Add one short sentence saying {name} received this conversation.'
    )
    reply = chat(prompt)
    print(f'{name}: {resp_text(reply)}')
    history = list(chat.hist)
    chat.close()

print([m['role'] for m in history])

title: remote
text:
Messages
fastllm represents a message as Msg(role, content=[Part, ...]). Each part has a type: text, thinking, tool_use, tool_result, input_image or input_audio. An image or audio part holds a data URL in part.text. rishi’s history uses OpenAI-shaped dicts.
to_msg converts one history message to a Msg. to_hist converts a Msg back and returns a list, because one tool Msg can hold several results.
The conversion keeps images and audio as data URLs. It does not replace them with placeholders, so media survives a move between backends. Thinking also survives. rishi stores it in channels['thought'], and fastllm stores it as a thinking part.
When a message mixes text and media, to_hist joins all the text into one part and puts it first. The test below shows this.


source

to_hist
def to_hist(
    m
):
Convert a fastllm Msg to a list of rishi history messages, since a tool Msg can hold several results.




source

to_msg
def to_msg(
    m
):
Convert one rishi history message to a fastllm Msg.



# a round trip through fastllm's Msg keeps text, thinking, tool calls and tool results intact
h = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'what is 2+2?'},
     {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'let me add', 'channels': {'thought': 'hmm'},
      'tool_calls': [ToolCall('add', {'a': 2, 'b': 2}, id='c1')]},
     {'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'c1', 'name': 'add', 'content': '4'},
     {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'it is 4'}]
msgs = [to_msg(m) for m in h]
test_eq([m.role for m in msgs], ['user', 'assistant', 'tool', 'assistant'])
back = [x for m in msgs for x in to_hist(m)]
test_eq(back[0], {'role': 'user', 'content': 'what is 2+2?'})
test_eq(back[1]['channels'], {'thought': 'hmm'})
test_eq(back[1]['tool_calls'][0].name, 'add')
test_eq(back[1]['tool_calls'][0].arguments, {'a': 2, 'b': 2})
test_eq(back[2], {'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'c1', 'name': 'add', 'content': '4'})
test_eq(back[3], {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'it is 4'})

# reverse conversion groups text first, then images and audio
mixed = [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'before'},
         {'type': 'image_url', 'image_url': {'url': 'data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo='}},
         {'type': 'image_url', 'image_url': {}},
         {'type': 'unknown'},
         {'type': 'text', 'text': 'between'},
         {'type': 'input_audio', 'input_audio': {'data': 'UklGRg==', 'format': 'wav'}},
         {'type': 'input_audio', 'input_audio': {}},
         {'type': 'text', 'text': 'after'}]
m = to_msg({'role': 'user', 'content': mixed})
test_eq([p.type for p in m.content], ['text', 'input_image', 'input_image', 'text', 'input_audio', 'input_audio', 'text'])
rt = to_hist(m)[0]
test_eq([p['type'] for p in rt['content']], ['text', 'image_url', 'image_url', 'input_audio', 'input_audio'])
test_eq(rt['content'][0]['text'], 'beforebetweenafter')
test_eq(rt['content'][1]['image_url']['url'], m.content[1].text)
test_eq(rt['content'][2]['image_url']['url'], m.content[2].text)
test_eq(rt['content'][3]['input_audio']['format'], 'wav')

# a server-side tool call keeps its flag across the hop
sm = to_msg({'role': 'assistant', 'content': '', 'tool_calls': [ToolCall('web_search', {}, id='s1', server=True)]})
assert to_hist(sm)[0]['tool_calls'][0].server

title: remote
text:
Responses and usage
norm_completion converts a fastllm Completion to a rishi Resp. It reads tool calls that the model wrote into its text as <tool_call> tags. It sets truncated when the reply hit the token limit. It adds token usage from norm_usage.
cached_tokens is set when the provider reports prompt caching. reasoning_tokens and cache_creation_tokens appear only when the provider reports them. A local backend’s usage dict does not change.
Some models generate images. fastllm’s message parts describe inputs only. gen_media searches the provider’s raw response for generated images in the shapes that Gemini, the OpenAI Responses and Images APIs, and LiteLLM use. norm_completion stores what it finds in Resp['media'] as {mime, data} dicts. It does not change the text.

Collect the images a model generated from the provider’s raw response, Completion.raw, as {mime, data} dicts.

    u, model:NoneType=None
):
Convert fastllm Usage to a rishi usage dict, keeping reasoning and cache-write counts when the provider reports them.



from base64 import b64encode

png = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + b'fake'
b64 = b64encode(png).decode()

# Gemini native, camelCase and snake_case, however deep the candidate sits
test_eq(gen_media({'candidates': [{'content': {'parts': [
    {'text': 'here you go'}, {'inlineData': {'mimeType': 'image/png', 'data': b64}}]}}]}),
    [{'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}])
test_eq(gen_media({'candidates': [{'content': {'parts': [
    {'inline_data': {'mime_type': 'image/webp', 'data': b64}}]}}]}),
    [{'mime': 'image/webp', 'data': png}])

# the OpenAI-shaped route litellm normalises Gemini's image output onto
test_eq(gen_media({'choices': [{'message': {'content': 'done',
    'images': [{'image_url': {'url': f'data:image/png;base64,{b64}'}}]}}]}),
    [{'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}])

# the Responses API image tool, and the Images API
test_eq(gen_media({'output': [{'type': 'image_generation_call', 'result': b64}]}),
        [{'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}])
test_eq(gen_media({'data': [{'b64_json': b64}]}), [{'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}])

# a plain text reply carries nothing, and neither does a missing `raw`
test_eq(gen_media({'choices': [{'message': {'content': 'just words'}}]}), [])
test_eq(gen_media(None), [])

# the same image reached by two routes in one payload is still one image
test_eq(len(gen_media({'candidates': [{'content': {'parts': [{'inlineData': {'mimeType': 'image/png', 'data': b64}}]}}],
                       'choices': [{'message': {'images': [{'image_url': {'url': f'data:image/png;base64,{b64}'}}]}}]})), 1)

# and it rides on `Resp.media`, leaving `content` alone
r = norm_completion(Completion(model='m', usage=Usage(prompt_tokens=1, completion_tokens=2),
        message=Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text(text='here')]),
        raw={'candidates': [{'content': {'parts': [{'inlineData': {'mimeType': 'image/png', 'data': b64}}]}}]}))
test_eq(r['content'], 'here')
test_eq(r['media'], [{'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}])

# a caller may hand in anything Completion-shaped; `raw` is newer than the function and
# must not become a requirement -- ramabana's routing test builds one without it
class _NoRaw:
    model, usage, finish_reason, tool_calls = 'm', None, 'stop', None
    message = Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text(text='hi')])
test_eq(norm_completion(_NoRaw())['content'], 'hi')
assert 'media' not in norm_completion(_NoRaw())

title: remote
text:
RemoteChat
RemoteChat runs fastllm’s async client from synchronous code. It uses Urai’s run_coro and sync_iter. With no model named, it uses dflt_remote, which is gpt-5.1.
max_output_tokens sets the output cap. Without it, the cap is the maximum that fastllm’s model table gives for the model. For a model that is not in the table, the cap is DFLT_MAX_TOKENS, 16,000. A reasoning model spends its thinking from the same cap. A small cap cut its tool calls short.
These options exist only on RemoteChat:

tool_choice forces one tool. The value 'required' forces any tool.
effort sets the provider’s reasoning effort. reasoning_effort is an accepted alias.
tool_mode='native' is the default. It sends tool schemas in the API’s tools field.
tool_mode='tags' writes the tool schemas into the system prompt and reads <tool_call> tags from the reply. Use it for a provider that has no tools field.
vendor_name and api_name override the vendor and the API that fastllm infers from the model id.

You can pass tool_mode for a single turn, streamed or not.
When the provider’s API lacks the effort level you set, the chat sends the level that EFFORT_MAP names. max becomes xhigh on OpenAI and Azure. xhigh and max become high on Gemini.
When a provider refuses the effort with a 400, the chat repeats the call once without it. dropped_effort then holds the reason, and the chat sends no effort. Set dropped_effort back to None to send effort again.
A one-shot call with think=False asks for NO_THINK_EFFORT, which is 'minimal'.
You can name a Gemini model with or without models/, as in gemini-3.5-flash, gemini/gemini-3.5-flash or models/gemini-3.5-flash. Gemini’s API puts the model in the URL and answers 404 without that prefix. The chat adds the prefix to the request. model_id stays as you gave it.
Some providers run tools on their own side, such as web search. Those calls come back marked server=True. The chat records them in the history. rishi does not run them.
A vendor in STREAM_ONLY answers only streamed requests. At present the only such vendor is codex. For it, the chat streams every request and collects the result.
Azure OpenAI’s v1 API works through base_url. Set these values:

base_url: https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1
model: the deployment name
api_key: the Azure key
api_name='openai' for the Responses API

The chat sends no api-version. The v1 API needs none.
On the chat-completions route, api_name='openai_chat', an Azure reasoning deployment refuses max_tokens. For a host in MAX_COMPLETION_HOSTS, the chat sends the output cap as max_completion_tokens. Every Azure model accepts that field.

def _add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    'Add a and b.'
    return a + b

# native puts the schemas on the wire; tags puts them in the system prompt and leaves the field empty
kw = RemoteChat('gpt-5.1', tools=[_add], sp='Be terse.')._kw()
test_eq([t['function']['name'] for t in kw['tools']], ['_add'])
test_eq(kw['system'], 'Be terse.')

kw = RemoteChat('gpt-5.1', tools=[_add], sp='Be terse.', tool_mode='tags', tool_choice='required')._kw()
assert 'tools' not in kw and 'tool_choice' not in kw
assert kw['system'].startswith('Be terse.') and '"name": "_add"' in kw['system']

# Parse tagged calls without dropping surrounding text.
def _comp(text):
    return Completion(model='m', usage=Usage(prompt_tokens=1, completion_tokens=2),
                      message=Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text(text=text)]))
r = norm_completion(_comp('on it\n<tool_call>{"name": "_add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}</tool_call>'))
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'on it')
test_eq((r['tool_calls'][0].name, r['tool_calls'][0].arguments), ('_add', {'a': 1, 'b': 2}))
test_eq(norm_completion(_comp('just prose')).get('tool_calls'), None)

# provider-billed reasoning and cache-write token counts appear only when the provider reports them
u = Usage(prompt_tokens=10, completion_tokens=5, cached_tokens=4, reasoning_tokens=7, cache_creation_tokens=3)
test_eq(norm_usage(u, 'm'), {'prompt_tokens': 10, 'completion_tokens': 5, 'total_tokens': 15,
                             'cached_tokens': 4, 'model': 'm', 'reasoning_tokens': 7, 'cache_creation_tokens': 3})
test_eq(set(norm_usage(Usage(prompt_tokens=1, completion_tokens=1), 'm')),
        {'prompt_tokens', 'completion_tokens', 'total_tokens', 'cached_tokens', 'model'})

us = UsageStats(**norm_usage(u)) + UsageStats(**norm_usage(u))
test_eq((us.reasoning_tokens, us.cache_creation_tokens, us.cached_tokens), (14, 6, 8))
assert 'reasoning=14' in repr(us) and 'cache_write=6' in repr(us)
test_eq(sum_usage([norm_usage(u), norm_usage(u)])['reasoning_tokens'], 14)
assert 'reasoning_tokens' not in sum_usage([{'prompt_tokens': 1}])   # absent, not zero, when nothing was reported


# codex answers a streamed request and refuses every other one (400 "Stream must be set to true"),
# so the calls that are not already streams have to be gathered from one
class _Stop(Exception): pass
def _fake(msgs, model, **kw):
    async def go(): raise _Stop(kw.get('stream'))
    return go()

def _streamed(chat, fn):
    try: fn(chat)
    except _Stop as e: return e.args[0]

_real, acomplete = acomplete, _fake
try:
    codex, plain = RemoteChat('codex/gpt-5.5'), RemoteChat('gpt-5.1')
    test_eq((codex._stream_only, plain._stream_only), (True, False))
    test_eq(_streamed(codex, lambda c: c._model_step()), True)
    test_eq(_streamed(plain, lambda c: c._model_step()), False)
    test_eq(_streamed(codex, lambda c: c._oneshot('hi')), True)
    test_eq(_streamed(codex, lambda c: c._structured_call('hi', _add, '')), True)
    test_eq(_streamed(plain, lambda c: c._structured_call('hi', _add, '')), False)
finally: acomplete = _real


# Azure's chat-completions route refuses `max_tokens` from a reasoning deployment, so the cap goes out as
# `max_completion_tokens` there; its Responses route and every other host keep `max_tokens`
az = 'https://res.openai.azure.com/openai/v1'
kw = RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url=az, api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat', max_output_tokens=900)._kw()
test_eq(('max_tokens' in kw, kw['xtra_body']), (False, {'max_completion_tokens': 900}))
kw = RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url=az, api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat', comp_kw={'xtra_body': {'store': False}})._kw()
mx54 = get_model_info('gpt-5.4')['max_output_tokens']   # a model fastllm knows asks for its own maximum
test_eq(kw['xtra_body'], {'max_completion_tokens': mx54, 'store': False})
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url=az, api_key='k', api_name='openai')._kw()['max_tokens'], mx54)
test_eq(RemoteChat('m', base_url='https://res.openai.azure.us/openai/v1', api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat')._max_completion, True)
test_eq(RemoteChat('m', base_url='https://api.example.com/v1', api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat')._kw()['max_tokens'], DFLT_MAX_TOKENS)

# the request itself: the deployment as the model, Bearer auth, `/openai/v1/responses`, no `api-version`
import fastllm.acomplete as fa
from fastllm.acomplete import mk_client
seen, _req = {}, fa.provider_req

    return {'output': [{'type': 'message', 'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'output_text', 'text': 'pong'}]}],
            'usage': {'input_tokens': 5, 'output_tokens': 1, 'total_tokens': 6}, 'status': 'completed'}
fa.provider_req = _fake_req
try: r = RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url=az, api_key='k', api_name='openai')('ping')
finally: fa.provider_req = _req
test_eq((seen['url'], seen['params'], seen['body']['model'], seen['body']['max_output_tokens']), (f'{az}/responses', None, 'gpt-5.4', mx54))
test_eq((resp_text(r), r['usage']['prompt_tokens']), ('pong', 5))
test_eq(mk_client('gpt-5.4', api_name='openai', api_key='k', base_url=az)[0].transport.base_headers['Authorization'], 'Bearer k')


A tool call that does not decode
fastllm decodes a model’s tool-call arguments before rishi sees the reply. It raises JSONDecodeError when the arguments are not whole JSON. The usual cause is the output cap: the model ran out of tokens while it wrote the call.
args_error checks that the error came from one of the fastllm functions in ARG_SITES. rishi raises any other decode error unchanged. cut_args tells a cut-off call from a malformed one.
A cut-off call goes back to the model with urai’s cut_msg_. The next step runs at CUT_CAP_MULT times the cap, up to the most that fastllm says the model can write. A malformed call goes back with the decoder’s error message.
A reply cut off while the model was still thinking, with no text and no call, goes back the same way and uses the same single resend. A second failure in the turn raises ToolCallError with the reason.

# a tool call cut off at the output cap, or not JSON at all, goes back to the model rather than killing the turn
# with fastllm's bare `JSONDecodeError`; the step after a cut-off call gets `CUT_CAP_MULT` times the cap
import fastllm.acomplete as fa
from fastcore.xtras import dict2obj
from urai import cut_msg_
def _wf(path: str, content: str) -> str:
    'Write content to path.'
    return f'wrote {len(content)}'
_CUT, _BAD, _OK = '{"path": "a.txt", "content": "it stops', '{"path": "a.txt" "content": "x"}', '{"path": "a.txt", "content": "whole"}'
def _resp(args):    # a Responses reply, its call cut short when `args` is
    if args is None: return {'output': [{'type': 'message', 'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'output_text', 'text': 'done'}]}], 'status': 'completed',
                             'usage': {'input_tokens': 5, 'output_tokens': 1, 'total_tokens': 6}}
    return {'output': [{'type': 'function_call', 'call_id': 'c1', 'id': 'fc1', 'name': '_wf', 'arguments': args}],
            'usage': {'input_tokens': 5, 'output_tokens': 9, 'total_tokens': 14}, 'status': 'incomplete' if args == _CUT else 'completed'}
def _cc(args):      # a chat-completions reply
    m = {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'done'} if args is None else {'role': 'assistant', 'content': None, 'tool_calls': [{'id': 'c1', 'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': '_wf', 'arguments': args}}]}
    return {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'message': m, 'finish_reason': 'stop' if args is None else 'length' if args == _CUT else 'tool_calls'}],
            'usage': {'prompt_tokens': 5, 'completion_tokens': 9, 'total_tokens': 14}}
def _chunks(args):  # a chat-completions stream: some prose, then the call in pieces, then `length` when it was cut
    yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'Writing it.'}}]}
    if args is None: yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {}, 'finish_reason': 'stop'}]}; return
    for i in range(0, len(args), 8):
        f = {'arguments': args[i:i+8]} | ({'name': '_wf'} if not i else {})
        yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {'tool_calls': [{'index': 0, 'id': 'c1' if not i else None, 'type': 'function', 'function': f}]}}]}
    yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {}, 'finish_reason': 'length' if args == _CUT else 'tool_calls'}]}
def _wire(*script):
    "A fake `provider_req` answering with `script` in order, and the request bodies it saw."
    bodies, it = [], iter(script)
    async def req(cli, path, body, params=None, stream=False, **kw):
        bodies.append(body); a = next(it)
        if isinstance(a, Exception): raise a
        if not stream: return dict2obj((_cc if 'chat' in path else _resp)(a))
        async def ev():
            for c in _chunks(a): yield dict2obj(c)
        return ev()
    return req, bodies
def _run(chat, *script, stream=False):
    req, bodies = _wire(*script)
    _req, fa.provider_req = fa.provider_req, req
    try: r = chat('go', stream=stream); r = ''.join(r) if stream else r
    finally: fa.provider_req = _req
    return r, bodies
_resps = lambda **kw: RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', api_key='k', tools=[_wf], max_output_tokens=1000, **kw)
_chats = lambda **kw: RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url='https://x.example.com/v1', api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat', tools=[_wf], max_output_tokens=1000, **kw)
caps = lambda bodies: [b.get('max_output_tokens') or b.get('max_tokens') or b.get('max_completion_tokens') for b in bodies]

# cut off, then asked again at four times the cap, then whole: the call runs, on both wires and both ways of sending
for mk, stream in ((_resps, False), (_resps, True), (_chats, False), (_chats, True)):
    if mk is _resps and stream: continue           # the Responses stream is fastllm's, covered by its own event parser
    c = mk()
    r, bodies = _run(c, _CUT, _OK, None, stream=stream)
    test_eq([m['role'] for m in c.hist], ['user', 'assistant', 'user', 'assistant', 'tool', 'assistant'])
    test_eq((c.hist[2]['content'], c.hist[4]['content']), (cut_msg_, 'wrote 5'))
    test_eq(caps(bodies), [1000, 4000, 1000])        # the raise lasts one step
    assert ('Writing it.' if stream else 'cut off at its 1000-token output limit') in c.hist[1]['content'] and 'lost' not in c.hist[1]   # what streamed, else why

# cut off twice: `ToolCallError` says what happened, not a decoder message
for mk, stream in ((_resps, False), (_chats, True)):
    test_fail(lambda: _run(mk(), _CUT, _CUT, stream=stream), contains="gpt-5.4's tool call was cut off at its 4000-token output limit")

# arguments that are not JSON go back naming the problem, at the same cap
c = _chats()
r, bodies = _run(c, _BAD, _OK, None, stream=True)
assert "not valid JSON (Expecting ',' delimiter at char 17)" in c.hist[2]['content']
test_eq((c.hist[4]['content'], caps(bodies)), ('wrote 5', [1000, 1000, 1000]))

# a `JSONDecodeError` that is not the model's, such as a proxy's HTML page, is raised as it was
test_fail(lambda: _run(_chats(), json.JSONDecodeError('Expecting value', '<html>', 0)), contains='Expecting value')

# the raise stays within what fastllm says the model can write; past that, the advice is smaller steps
c = RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', max_output_tokens=100_000)
assert 'ask for smaller steps' in c._cut(100_000) and c._boost == get_model_info('gpt-5.4')['max_output_tokens']
c = RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', max_output_tokens=128_000)
assert 'raise max_output_tokens' not in c._cut(128_000) and c._boost is None
c = RemoteChat('no-such-model', base_url='https://x.example.com/v1', api_key='k', max_output_tokens=500); c._cut(500); test_eq(c._boost, 2000)

# a reply that is all thinking when the cap cuts it goes back once at the raised cap, then raises
_THINK = 'think'
_r0, _c0 = _resp, _chunks
def _resp(args):
    if args != _THINK: return _r0(args)
    return {'output': [{'type': 'reasoning', 'id': 'r1', 'summary': []}], 'status': 'incomplete', 'incomplete_details': {'reason': 'max_output_tokens'},
            'usage': {'input_tokens': 5, 'output_tokens': 1000, 'total_tokens': 1005}}
def _chunks(args):
    if args != _THINK: yield from _c0(args); return
    yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {'role': 'assistant', 'content': ''}}]}
    yield {'choices': [{'index': 0, 'delta': {}, 'finish_reason': 'length'}]}
for mk, stream in ((_resps, False), (_chats, True)):
    c = mk()
    r, bodies = _run(c, _THINK, None, stream=stream)
    test_eq((c.hist[-1]['content'], caps(bodies)), ('Writing it.' if stream else 'done', [1000, 4000]))
    assert 'still thinking' in c.hist[1]['content'] and 'channels' not in c.hist[1] and 'thinking less' in c.hist[2]['content']
    test_fail(lambda: _run(mk(), _THINK, _THINK, stream=stream), contains='gpt-5.4 was still thinking when its reply was cut off at its 4000-token output limit')

# the default cap: the model's own maximum, `DFLT_MAX_TOKENS` for a model fastllm does not know, and `max_output_tokens` over both
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4').max_output_tokens, get_model_info('gpt-5.4')['max_output_tokens'])
test_eq(RemoteChat('no-such-model', base_url='https://x.example.com/v1', api_key='k').max_output_tokens, DFLT_MAX_TOKENS)
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', max_output_tokens=900).max_output_tokens, 900)
assert DFLT_MAX_TOKENS >= 16_000

# tags mode: a `<tool_call>` cut off at the cap keeps `unread`, so it is asked for again, not run with no arguments
r = norm_completion(Completion(model='m', finish_reason='length', message=Msg(role='assistant', content=[Text(text='<tool_call>{"name": "_wf", "arguments": {"path": "a')])))
test_eq((r['truncated'], r['tool_calls'][0].get('unread')), (True, True))

# `ask(schema=)`: once more at the raised cap, then `ToolCallError`
c = _resps()
req, bodies = _wire(_CUT, _OK); _req, fa.provider_req = fa.provider_req, req
try: test_eq(c._structured_call('go', _wf, ''), {'path': 'a.txt', 'content': 'whole'})
finally: fa.provider_req = _req
test_eq(caps(bodies), [1000, 4000])
req, bodies = _wire(_CUT, _CUT); _req, fa.provider_req = fa.provider_req, req
try: test_fail(lambda: c._structured_call('go', _wf, ''), contains='cut off at its 1000-token output limit')
finally: fa.provider_req = _req


# a Gemini model reaches `v1beta/models/<id>`, however it was named: without `models/` Gemini answers 404
import fastllm.acomplete as fa
seen, _req = [], fa.provider_req
async def _gem_req(cli, path, body, params=None, stream=False, **kw):
    seen.append(cli._url(path))
    return {'candidates': [{'content': {'role': 'model', 'parts': [{'text': 'pong'}]}, 'finishReason': 'STOP'}],
            'usageMetadata': {'promptTokenCount': 5, 'candidatesTokenCount': 1, 'totalTokenCount': 6}}
gem = 'https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-3.5-flash:generateContent'
fa.provider_req = _gem_req
try:
    for m in ('gemini-3.5-flash', 'gemini/gemini-3.5-flash', 'models/gemini-3.5-flash', 'gemini/models/gemini-3.5-flash'):
        seen.clear(); c = RemoteChat(m, api_key='k')
        r = c('ping')

        assert r['usage']['prompt_tokens'] == 5, r['usage']
    for kw in (dict(vendor_name='gemini'), dict(vendor_name='gemini', base_url='https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/')):   # a named route: `acomplete` keeps the vendor prefix, so it goes here
        seen.clear(); RemoteChat('gemini/gemini-3.5-flash', api_key='k', **kw)('ping'); test_eq(seen, [gem])
    seen.clear(); RemoteChat('gemini-3.5-flash', api_key='k', api_name='gemini', base_url='https://gw.example.com/')('ping')
    test_eq(seen, ['https://gw.example.com/v1beta/models/gemini-3.5-flash:generateContent'])
    seen.clear(); RemoteChat('tunedModels/mine', api_key='k', vendor_name='gemini')('ping')
    test_eq(seen, ['https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/tunedModels/mine:generateContent'])
finally: fa.provider_req = _req
test_eq(RemoteChat('gemini-3.5-flash', base_url='https://gw.example.com/v1', api_key='k')._wire_model, 'gemini-3.5-flash')   # an OpenAI-shaped route takes the bare id
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4')._wire_model, 'gpt-5.4')
test_eq(RemoteChat('gemini-3.5-flash')._kw(stream=True)['stream'], True)

test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='max')._kw()['reasoning_effort'], 'xhigh')
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4', base_url=az, api_key='k', api_name='openai_chat', effort='max')._kw()['reasoning_effort'], 'xhigh')
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini')._kw(effort='max')['reasoning_effort'], 'xhigh')    # per turn too
test_eq(RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='xhigh')._kw()['reasoning_effort'], 'xhigh')
test_eq(RemoteChat('anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5', effort='max')._kw()['reasoning_effort'], 'max')
test_eq(RemoteChat('models/gemini-3.5-flash', effort='max')._kw()['reasoning_effort'], 'high')

# a 400 that names the effort: the call goes once more without it, and `dropped_effort` says why
class _E400(Exception): status_code = 400
def _fake(msgs, model, **kw):
    sent.append(kw.get('reasoning_effort'))
    async def go():
        if kw.get('reasoning_effort'): raise _E400("Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'xhigh' with this model.")
        return _comp('pong')
    async def gen():
        if kw.get('reasoning_effort'): raise _E400('400 Bad Request: reasoning.effort is not supported')
        yield Text(text='po'); yield Text(text='ng'); yield _comp('pong')
    if not kw.get('stream'): return go()
    async def wrap(): return gen()
    return wrap()

_real, acomplete = acomplete, _fake
try:
    sent, c = [], RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='max')
    test_eq((resp_text(c('ping')), sent), ('pong', ['xhigh', None]))
    assert 'refused reasoning effort' in c.dropped_effort and 'xhigh' in c.dropped_effort, c.dropped_effort
    sent.clear(); c('again')
    test_eq(sent, [None])                         # while it is set, no effort goes out
    sent, s = [], RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='high')
    test_eq((''.join(s('ping', stream=True)), sent, bool(s.dropped_effort)), ('pong', ['high', None], True))
    def _other(msgs, model, **kw):
        async def go(): raise _E400('400 Bad Request: messages is empty')
        return go()
    acomplete = _other
    test_fail(lambda: RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='high')('ping'), contains='messages is empty')   # any other 400 is the caller's
    def _rs(msgs, model, **kw):
        async def go(): raise _E400("Item 'rs_0a1b' of type 'reasoning' was provided without its required following item.")
        return go()
    acomplete, c = _rs, RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='high')
    test_fail(lambda: c('ping'), contains="type 'reasoning'")     # a reasoning item, not the effort
    test_eq(c.dropped_effort, None)
    class _E500(Exception): status_code = 500
    def _down(msgs, model, **kw):
        async def go(): raise _E500('upstream said 400 times: reasoning_effort timed out')
        return go()
    acomplete, c = _down, RemoteChat('gpt-5.4-mini', effort='high')
    test_fail(lambda: c('ping'), contains='upstream')               # only a 400 status counts, not "400" in the text
    test_eq(c.dropped_effort, None)
finally: acomplete = _real

# a turn's own `tool_mode` decides whether the stream is split on tags, as it decides where the schemas go
call = 'on it\n<' + 'tool_call>{"name": "_add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}</' + 'tool_call>'
def _tagged(msgs, model, **kw):
    async def gen():
        yield Text(text=call); yield _comp(call)

_real, acomplete = acomplete, _tagged
try:

finally: acomplete = _real

class _HTTPErr(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code, msg): super().__init__(msg); self.status_code = code

def _failing(code, msg, sent):
    async def collect(msgs, **kw): sent.append(kw.get('reasoning_effort')); raise _HTTPErr(code, msg)
    return collect

rc, sent = RemoteChat('gpt-4o', key='k'), []

test_eq(len(sent), 1)
rc._collect = _failing(400, 'Unsupported reasoning_effort', sent := [])

text:
The wire
A turn either sends a message to a live Claude Code session or resumes a filed transcript with one query call. rishi calls the system prompt the briefing. It goes to Claude Code through Claude Code’s own system-prompt option.
By default, your tools travel as tags in the prompt. A managed MCP policy cannot remove them. Pass mcp_servers when Claude Code must reach an MCP server itself. Those tools run on Claude Code’s side, outside rishi’s approval, budget and result-length limits. rishi reports their calls in Resp.channels['server_tools'].
These defaults keep the backend working on locked-down machines:

strict_mcp_config is off. Enterprise configurations reject that flag.
api_key=False blanks ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the subprocess environment. The session then bills your subscription, not the API. api_key=True leaves the variable as it is.
max_buffer sets the limit on Claude Code’s output. The SDK rejects output that exceeds the configured limit instead of truncating it.




limit
bytes




SDK default
1 MiB (1048576)


MAX_BUFFER, the rishi default for max_buffer
10 MiB (10485760)



The constants below are pinned model ids. claude_model accepts the short keys of CLAUDE_MODELS, such as 'opus5'. It passes the CLI’s own aliases (opus, sonnet, haiku, fable) through unchanged. Each alias follows the newest model of its tier on your plan. With no model, a chat uses opus5, which is claude-opus-5.
norm_claude converts Claude Code’s result to a Resp. A failed turn raises ClaudeError. ClaudeError carries the HTTP status when one can be found, and a caller can use it to decide whether to retry. A cancelled turn is not an error. The reply is whatever arrived before the cancel.
claude_version asks the binary for its version and gives it /dev/null as stdin. Claude Code is a Node program. A Node program that shares the caller’s terminal can leave the terminal non-blocking.

test_eq(claude_model('opus5'), opus5)             # a `CLAUDE_MODELS` key, resolved
test_eq(claude_model(opus5), opus5)               # a pinned id, untouched

test_eq(claude_model('', dflt=None), None)
test_eq(claude_fallback('opus5,haiku'), f'{opus5},haiku')     # a chain, in the order it is tried
test_eq(claude_fallback(['sonnet46', '', 'haiku45']), f'{sonnet46},{haiku45}')

# the version a record claims is the binary's, not a constant that goes stale under it
test_eq(re.fullmatch(r'\d+\.\d+\.\d+', claude_version()) is not None, True)
test_eq(claude_version('definitely-not-the-claude-binary'), ant.CC_VERSION)   # nothing to ask
# the probe reads end of file, so a line waiting on the caller's terminal stays there and the terminal stays blocking
import os, pty, sys, tempfile
fake = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'claude'
fake.write_text(f'#!{sys.executable}\nimport os; t = os.isatty(0); os.set_blocking(0, False); print(f"{{int(t)}}.0.0")\n'); fake.chmod(0o755)
m, s = pty.openpty(); os.write(m, b'x\n')
probe = f"import os, select; from rishi.claude import claude_version; print(claude_version({str(fake)!r}), os.get_blocking(0), os.read(0, 9) if select.select([0], [], [], 1)[0] else b'')"
got = subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', probe], stdin=s, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60).stdout.split()
os.close(s); os.close(m)
test_eq(got, ['0.0.0', 'True', "b'x\\n'"])

r = norm_claude({'result': 'ok\n<tool_call>\n{"name": "ls", "arguments": {"path": "."}}\n</tool_call>',
                 'usage': {'input_tokens': 10, 'output_tokens': 5, 'cache_read_input_tokens': 90,

test_eq(resp_text(r), 'ok')
test_eq(r['tool_calls'][0]['function']['name'], 'ls')
test_eq(r['usage']['total_tokens'], 112)          # cache reads and writes are prompt tokens too
test_eq(r['usage']['cache_creation_tokens'], 7)
test_eq(r['usage']['cost'], 0.0042)               # what Claude Code itself billed, not a price table
assert 'reasoning_tokens' not in r['usage']       # not reported, so not claimed as 0
# thinking is part of `output_tokens`, counted again under `output_tokens_details`
th = norm_claude_usage({'input_tokens': 2, 'output_tokens': 840, 'output_tokens_details': {'thinking_tokens': 711}})
test_eq((th['completion_tokens'], th['reasoning_tokens']), (840, 711))

# Preserve status for retry policy.
try:
    norm_claude({'is_error': True, 'result': 'API Error: 429 rate limited'}); assert False, 'no raise'
except ClaudeError as e:
    test_eq(e.status, 429)
    test_eq(e.raw['is_error'], True)
try:                                              # a reported status wins over one read out of the text
    norm_claude({'is_error': True, 'result': 'failed after 500 attempts', 'api_error_status': 529})
except ClaudeError as e: test_eq(e.status, 529)
try:                                              # ...and no status at all is not an error
    norm_claude({'is_error': True, 'subtype': 'error_during_execution'})

    norm_claude({'is_error': True, 'result': 'nope', 'api_error_status': 'rate_limit'})

tpe = {'is_error': True, 'result': "The model's tool call could not be parsed (retry also failed).", 'usage': {}}

title: claude
text:
Options
Claude Code has tools of its own, such as Bash and Edit. These rules decide which of them a chat can use:

A chat that carries rishi tools switches all Claude Code tools off. Your tools are the only ones Claude can call.
A chat with no rishi tools keeps Claude Code’s default set, minus claude_disallowed. By default claude_disallowed holds Bash, Write, Edit and NotebookEdit.
claude_tools=[] switches all Claude Code tools off and gives plain completions.
bare=True, the default, stops Claude Code from loading project instructions (CLAUDE.md), skills, plugins and hooks. It does not restrict tools.

tool_mode='native' sends rishi’s tools through an in-process MCP server, not through the prompt. See Native tool calls.
claude_server_tools switches on Claude Code’s web tools, WebSearch and WebFetch. They run on Claude Code’s side.
fallback names a model, or a list of models tried in order. Claude Code uses them when the chosen model is overloaded or retired.
set_model switches the model of a live session without rebuilding the history.
effort sets the reasoning effort: low, medium, high, xhigh or max. It is the only generation setting that Claude Code takes. The chat ignores temperature, token limits and similar options.
When the effort of a call differs from the effort the live session opened with, the chat reconnects the session and resumes it from hist. A call with no effort runs at the chat’s own effort and reconnects in the same way.

Pictures and documents
Claude Code takes Anthropic content blocks. rishi converts its OpenAI-shaped history with aidialog and fastllm. An image becomes an image block. A PDF becomes a document block. A live session and a filed transcript both carry these blocks.
With stateful=False, transcript=False, the chat flattens the history into one text prompt. A text prompt cannot hold an image, so the chat refuses media. Claude Code takes no audio on any path.

title: claude
text:
Transcript records
Claude Code resumes a session from a JSONL transcript at ~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<id>.jsonl. anth_msgs converts rishi’s history into Anthropic messages. llmsurgery.ant writes them as transcript records. anth_blocks keeps images and documents as typed blocks.
The chat files tool calls in the form that the session uses.
On the default tags channel, tag_calls files a call as <tool_call> text and files its result as prose. render_prompt sends them in the same form in a live session. Filing them as native tool_use blocks failed. A resumed session saw tools that the options no longer declared, and it ended its next turn after one sentence.
On the native channel, the chat files calls and results as tool_use and tool_result blocks. tu_id rewrites each id into Anthropic’s toolu_ form so that every pair matches. A tool that returned nothing is filed as (no output). The API rejects empty text blocks.
The chat always files assistant content as a list of blocks. Claude Code 2.1.238 calls .some() on it, and a plain string crashes it.
A session id is a hash of the messages plus a random value that is unique to each chat. Refiling the same chat gives the same id. Two chats that hold the same conversation get different files, and neither deletes the other’s file during cleanup.
A chat removes the transcripts it filed when it closes, unless cleanup=False. prune_sessions clears old transcripts that remain. Each record carries the version that the installed claude --version reports.
Two settings decide how the conversation travels:

stateful=True, the default, keeps one Claude Code process for the chat. It sends tool results mid-turn as text.
stateful=False starts a fresh query each turn and refiles the whole history as typed records. Adding transcript=False sends the history as one flattened text prompt, which cannot carry media.

Session watermark
During a tool turn, the chat appends Claude’s reply and then the tool results to hist. The live session already holds its own reply. Sending the reply back would make Claude read its own words as new input.

title: claude
text:
Native tool calls
With tool_mode='native', rishi’s tools reach Claude as MCP tools, not as prompt text. The chat declares an in-process MCP server named rishi (RISHI_MCP). The server holds one tool per toolspec, with the toolspec’s JSON schema and descriptions. Only those tools are allowed, as mcp__rishi__NAME. Claude Code’s own tools stay off. The schemas leave the system prompt.
In this mode Claude Code runs the tool loop itself. One model step can hold several calls. Each call passes through the same pieces of Urai’s loop as a tagged call:

_approve1 applies the approval gate, the step budget and before_tool_calls.
call_tool runs the tool.
_record_tool truncates the result to tool_max_len and applies after_tool_calls.

The chat writes the call and its result to hist. Transcripts, resumes and callbacks see them as they see tagged calls.
Calls run one at a time. Each call runs in a worker thread, inside a copy of the context of the thread that started the step. Context variables therefore reach the tool and the approver. The silence timer waits while a tool runs.
A refused call, a spent budget and a cancelled turn each answer Claude with the reason. A spent budget also interrupts the live session. A turn that ran a native tool is never tried again after a stall.
A machine with an enterprise MCP configuration refuses every MCP server a program declares. There the chat raises ClaudeMcpRefused, a ClaudeError that carries Claude Code’s own message. The caller can then switch to tool_mode='tags'. A tool name longer than MCP_NAME_MAX, 64 characters with the prefix, raises ValueError.

title: claude
text:
Silence
Claude Code streams token deltas, so a working turn is never quiet for long. A turn that sends nothing at all, not even a stream event, for timeout seconds (240 by default) is stuck. _drain closes the stream, which ends the SDK’s query and its subprocess, and raises ClaudeStall. _with_retry then disconnects a live session, passes a status note to on_stall, and tries the turn once more.
What the retry sends depends on what was already shown:

Nothing yet, or only thinking: the same turn again, from the same filed conversation. The thinking may show twice.
Text: that text is not sent again. It is filed as the reply so far, and a fresh query asks Claude Code to finish it with STALL_PROMPT. Only the continuation streams, and the turn’s result is the shown text plus the continuation.
A call to one of Claude Code’s own tools: no retry. A replay would run the tool again. The stall is raised.
A native tool call: the timer waits while the tool runs. After one has run, a stall is raised and not retried.
A whole tool call in the text: the turn ends there with that text, as it would have, and a live session reconnects on the next turn.

A failure while connecting gets the same one retry, with a status note to on_stall. On a live session, that is client.connect() failing with a CLIConnectionError or not finishing in timeout seconds. On a query, it is the same error, or Claude Code’s initialize request timing out, before any message arrives. Nothing has run at that point, so nothing is replayed. A missing claude binary (CLINotFoundError), a refusal of rishi’s MCP server, and any other error are raised at once. Another try would fail the same way.
Each wire call has one retry, shared by a failed connect, a stall and a session that died before it said anything. After a connect is retried, a stall is raised, not retried. A failed connect on the retry that follows a stall raises the connect error. A cancelled turn is never retried.
If the retry goes silent too, ClaudeStall names the limit and timeout_hint, which says how the caller raises it. The stalled attempt sent no result, so its tokens and cost are not counted. _oneshot is not retried.

text:
Tests
The tests below check the SDK options, the transcript records, which chat owns which session file, and the boundary between the tool channels. None of them starts Claude Code.

def _fn(query: str) -> str:
    "Search the code."
    return ''

c = ClaudeChat('claude/claude-opus-5', sp='be brief', tools=[_fn], claude_disallowed=('Bash',))
c.hist = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'what is 2 plus 2?'}]
test_eq(c.model_id, 'claude-opus-5')          # the `claude/` prefix is stripped, the id is not
test_eq(ClaudeChat('claude/opus5').model_id, opus5)     # ...and a short name is resolved to one
test_eq(ClaudeChat('claude/sonnet').model_id, 'sonnet')  # the CLI's alias travels as written
test_eq(c.local, False)

o = c._opts(c._sp())
# The enterprise contract: no dynamic server is declared, and `strict_mcp_config` is *not* claimed.
# A managed machine refuses that flag outright, so asking for it is how this path used to fail.
test_eq(o.mcp_servers, {})
test_eq(o.strict_mcp_config, False)
test_eq(o.model, 'claude-opus-5')
test_eq(o.disallowed_tools, ['Bash'])
# rishi's tools are the only tool channel: Claude Code's own are off while this chat carries any
test_eq(o.tools, [])
test_eq(ClaudeChat()._opts('').tools, None)   # with none of rishi's, its own are left as they were

# ...so the schemas have to be somewhere, and the system prompt is where
test_eq('be brief' in o.system_prompt and '"_fn"' in o.system_prompt and '<tool_call>' in o.system_prompt, True)
test_eq('be brief' not in c._prompt(), True)  # and the briefing is not also in the conversation
test_eq(c.tool_channel, 'tags')

# an ambient API key never reaches the subprocess: it would silently meter a subscription session
test_eq(o.env, {'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY': ''})
test_eq(ClaudeChat(api_key=True)._opts('').env, {})
# the SDK's own 1MB stdout cap raises rather than truncating, losing a long reply outright
test_eq(o.max_buffer_size, MAX_BUFFER)
# the Claude Code on $PATH runs, not the SDK's bundled copy, which lags and refuses newer models
test_eq(o.cli_path, shutil.which(CLAUDE_BIN))
test_eq(ClaudeChat(bin='definitely-not-the-claude-binary')._opts('').cli_path, None)
# the harness's own context is off by default: this is a model, not the user's IDE agent
test_eq((o.setting_sources, o.skills), ([], []))
test_eq(ClaudeChat(bare=False)._opts('').setting_sources, None)

# Claude Code's web tools are the one place its own tools are a feature, and they are opt-in
w = ClaudeChat(claude_server_tools=CLAUDE_SERVER_TOOLS)._opts('')
test_eq(w.tools, ['WebFetch', 'WebSearch'])
test_eq(w.allowed_tools, list(CLAUDE_SERVER_TOOLS))

# the conversation is resumed from a file, and the session's own turns stay out of that file
o2 = c._opts('', resume=c._file_sess([{'role': 'user', 'content': 'earlier'}]), fork=True)
test_eq(o2.fork_session, True)
assert o2.resume, 'no session to resume'
test_eq(ClaudeChat(transcript=False)._file_sess([{'role': 'user', 'content': 'x'}]), None)

# transcripts stay out of a real project unless you name one
test_eq(ClaudeChat()._cwd, CLAUDE_WORK_DIR.resolve())
test_eq(ClaudeChat(workspace='.')._cwd, Path('.').resolve())

# an overloaded or retired model moves down the chain instead of ending the turn
test_eq(ClaudeChat(fallback='sonnet46')._opts('').fallback_model, sonnet46)
test_eq(ClaudeChat(fallback=['opus', 'haiku45'])._opts('').fallback_model, f'opus,{haiku45}')
test_eq(o.fallback_model, None)               # and no chain by default: one model, or a failed turn

# the model can change mid-conversation. With no session live that is just the next turn's option
m = ClaudeChat(sonnet46)
test_eq(m.set_model('haiku45'), haiku45)
test_eq(m._opts('').model, haiku45)
test_eq(m.set_model(), None)                  # ...and `None` hands the choice back to Claude Code
test_eq(m._opts('').model, None)

text:
MCP servers
Pass mcp_servers when Claude Code must reach an MCP server itself. Every tool of each named server is allowed unless mcp_tools narrows the list. These tools run inside Claude Code, outside rishi’s tool loop. rishi reports their calls in Resp.channels['server_tools'], not in tool_calls. Nothing waits on rishi to answer them.

import claude_agent_sdk as _sdk


srv = {'files': {'type': 'stdio', 'command': 'nothing-runs-here'}}

# Nothing named, nothing declared: byte for byte the enterprise default above.
test_eq(ClaudeChat()._opts('').mcp_servers, {})
test_eq(ClaudeChat().mcp_toolnames, [])

# Named servers are declared, and every tool of each is allowed unless the caller narrows it.
m = ClaudeChat(tools=[_fn], mcp_servers=srv)
test_eq(m.mcp_toolnames, ['mcp__files'])
o = m._opts('')
test_eq(o.mcp_servers, srv)
test_eq(o.allowed_tools, ['mcp__files'])
test_eq(o.tools, ['mcp__files'])              # available: these, and not Claude Code's own set

n = ClaudeChat(mcp_servers=srv, mcp_tools=['mcp__files__read'])
test_eq(n._opts('').allowed_tools, ['mcp__files__read'])
test_eq(ClaudeChat(mcp_servers=srv, mcp_tools=[])._opts('').allowed_tools, [])

# `strict_mcp_config` stays off unless asked for. It is refused where an enterprise config exists.
test_eq(m._opts('').strict_mcp_config, False)
test_eq(ClaudeChat(mcp_servers=srv, strict_mcp_config=True)._opts('').strict_mcp_config, True)

# Native mode carries rishi's tools on its own MCP server, so the prompt carries no schemas.
t = ClaudeChat(sp='be brief', tools=[_fn], mcp_servers=srv, tool_mode='native')
test_eq(t.tool_channel, 'native')
test_eq(ClaudeChat().tool_channel, 'tags')    # `tool_mode` unset is the enterprise default
test_eq(t._sp(), 'be brief')                  # no schemas, because they travel somewhere else
assert '<tool_call>' in ClaudeChat(sp='be brief', tools=[_fn])._sp()

# A tool Claude Code ran on its own side is a report, not a call rishi has to answer.
use = claude_tool_use(_sdk.ToolUseBlock(id='t1', name='mcp__files__read', input={'p': 'x'}), _sdk)
test_eq(use, {'id': 't1', 'name': 'mcp__files__read', 'server': 'files', 'input': {'p': 'x'}})
test_eq(claude_tool_use(_sdk.ToolUseBlock(id='t2', name='WebSearch', input={}), _sdk)['server'], '')
test_eq(claude_tool_use(_sdk.TextBlock(text='hello'), _sdk), None)

r = norm_claude({'result': 'done', 'usage': {}, 'server_tools': [use]})
test_eq(r['channels']['server_tools'], [use])
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'done')
test_eq('tool_calls' in r, False)             # nothing here is waiting on rishi
test_eq(norm_claude({'result': 'done', 'usage': {}}).get('channels'), None)


A tagged tool round trip
Claude receives rishi’s tool schemas in the system prompt. When it writes a tagged call, norm_claude converts the tag to an ordinary tool call. Urai’s tool loop runs the Python function and records the result. Claude then writes the final reply. This test scripts the two replies from Claude. The parser, the tool loop, the function call and the history are real.


Against Claude Code with tagged tools
This cell uses the default live session. Claude receives the tool schema through _sp() and writes a tagged call. rishi parses the tag, runs the Python function and sends the result back to the same Claude Code session. The cell needs a signed-in Claude Code installation. The test run skips it.

from rishi.claude import ClaudeChat
from urai import resp_text
live_tag_calls = []
def live_tag_add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    "Add two integers and record the call."
    live_tag_calls.append((a, b))
    return a + b

live_tag = ClaudeChat('haiku', tools=[live_tag_add], default_cbs=False)
live_tag_reply = live_tag('Use live_tag_add once with a=2 and b=3. Then answer with only the result.')
assert live_tag_calls == [(2, 3)]
assert '5' in resp_text(live_tag_reply)
assert [m['role'] for m in live_tag.hist] == ['user', 'assistant', 'tool', 'assistant']
assert live_tag.hist[2]['content'] == '5'
assert live_tag.hist[2]['tool_call_id'] == live_tag.hist[1]['tool_calls'][0]['id']
assert 'server_tools' not in (live_tag_reply.get('channels') or {})
live_tag.close()



MCP events from the SDK
MCP tools run inside Claude Code, not in Urai’s tool loop. _sdk_events picks up the SDK’s ToolUseBlock for each such call and passes it through to the final result. This test replaces the SDK’s query iterator, so no MCP server runs and Claude is not contacted.


A reply that goes on past its own tool call
A model can write a tool call and keep going in the same response as though the call had been answered. It writes more calls, then findings it never saw. Claude Code’s result holds only the last text block. Without a guard, the calls were lost and the invented findings reached the caller as the answer.
_drain stops at the first text block that holds a call. rishi shows and keeps nothing after that block. The turn’s text is what came before the stop. The call runs, and its real result comes back.


Against Claude Code and a local MCP server
This cell gives Claude Code a real MCP server running inside the Python process. Claude chooses and runs the MCP tool. The assertions check that the Python handler ran and that rishi received Claude Code’s report of the call. The cell needs a signed-in Claude Code installation. The test run skips it.

from claude_agent_sdk import create_sdk_mcp_server, tool

mcp_calls = []
@tool('add', 'Add two integers.', {'a': int, 'b': int})
async def mcp_add(args):
    mcp_calls.append((args['a'], args['b']))
    return {'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': str(args['a'] + args['b'])}]}

calc = create_sdk_mcp_server('calc', tools=[mcp_add])
live_mcp = ClaudeChat('haiku', mcp_servers={'calc': calc}, mcp_tools=['mcp__calc__add'],
                      stateful=False, transcript=False, default_cbs=False)
live_reply = live_mcp('Use the calc add tool once with a=2 and b=3. Then answer with only the result.')
assert mcp_calls == [(2, 3)]
assert resp_text(live_reply).strip() == '5'
assert [x['name'] for x in live_reply['channels']['server_tools']] == ['mcp__calc__add']
live_mcp.close()

core
text:
The shared layer
Backend modules import the shared types, such as Chat, ChatOpts and Resp, from urai directly. The tests below check that importing rishi.core registers the runtimes and does not copy Urai’s namespace.
RishiToolLoop is the base class for the backends that drive Urai’s tool loop. These are llama.cpp, MLX, Ollama, the hosted API and Claude Code. Copilot uses it through the hosted API class. LiteRT-LM does not use it, because the LiteRT-LM engine runs tools itself. RishiToolLoop turns on three callbacks by default. UsageCallback counts token usage. ToolReminderCallback reminds the model which tools it has. SlidingWindowCallback removes old messages when the context window is full.
split_model_path turns a model name into a Hugging Face repo id or a local file path. It removes any runtime prefix first. An explicit model_path argument takes priority over a path in the name. The LiteRT-LM, llama.cpp and MLX backends call it. The Ollama backend does not.

import importlib, importlib.util
import rishi, rishi.core, urai

test_eq(rishi.Chat is urai.Chat, True)
test_eq(hasattr(rishi.core, 'Chat'), False)
for mod in ('llama', 'mlx', 'remote', 'claude', 'copilot', 'ollama'):
    if mod == 'mlx' and not importlib.util.find_spec('mlx'): continue   # Apple Silicon only
    public = importlib.import_module(f'rishi.{mod}').__all__
    assert 'Chat' not in public and 'UsageStats' not in public


test_eq(split_model_path(None), (None, None))
test_eq(split_model_path('mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit'), ('mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit', None))
test_eq(split_model_path('mlx/mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit'), ('mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit', None))
test_eq(split_model_path('model.gguf'), (None, 'model.gguf'))
test_eq(split_model_path('repo/id', 'given/path.gguf'), ('repo/id', 'given/path.gguf'))

Model capabilities
A Caps record lists the kinds of input and output a model takes. You can check it before you send a picture to a model. Urai reads the Caps record of a hosted model from the fastllm model table. Local models have no such table. Each local runtime supplies a function that inspects the model. litert_caps reports text, image and audio for every LiteRT-LM model. LiteRT-LM builds the vision and audio encoders whenever multimodal input is on. ollama_caps_ asks the Ollama daemon, which holds the model weights.

title: core
text:
The seven backends
BACKENDS holds one Runtime record per backend. A record has the backend name, the class that implements it, a capabilities function, and the name patterns that identify its models. Urai imports the class when the backend is first used. When Chat gets a model name and no runtime, Urai tries the patterns in list order and takes the first match. Ollama comes before llama.cpp in the list. The id hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3-4B-GGUF contains gguf, but it is an Ollama id and not a file for llama.cpp. LiteRT-LM is the default when no model is named.
Claude Code and Copilot have no patterns, because their model names look like hosted model names. Choose them with a claude/ or copilot/ prefix, or with runtime='claude' or runtime='copilot'. The tests below show which names go to which backend. A name that matches no pattern raises an error.

test_eq(list(RUNTIMES), ['litert', 'ollama', 'llama', 'mlx', 'remote', 'claude', 'copilot'])
test_eq(infer_runtime('gemma-3n-E4B.litertlm'), 'litert')
test_eq(infer_runtime('hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3-4B-GGUF'), 'ollama')   # asked before llama

test_eq(infer_runtime('mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit'), 'mlx')
test_eq(infer_runtime('gpt-5.1'), 'remote')
