Loading GGUF models
You name a model by its Hub repo id, such as Qwen/Qwen3-4B-GGUF, and rishi picks the file. The constants below are ready-made repo ids. Qwen3 models can think before answering and write tool calls in a format llama.cpp already parses. Any GGUF repo works.
A repo often holds one file per quantization, plus an mmproj file. That file is the projector, a small separate model that turns images or audio into input the language model can read. get_model finds the model file in three steps. It uses a model_path you pass if the file exists. Otherwise it searches the local Hugging Face cache without using the network. Otherwise it downloads the file. It prefers the quant you ask for, Q4_K_M by default, and falls back to the first .gguf file. It never picks the projector. It raises FileNotFoundError when the repo has no model file. cached_model is the cache step on its own and returns None on a miss. The old names _get_model and _cached_model still work. get_mmproj finds the projector the same way, for vision and audio models. It raises FileNotFoundError when the repo has no projector. DFLT_N_CTX is the context window an engine gets when nothing else sets one, 8192 tokens.
gpu_offload_supported says whether the installed llama-cpp-python wheel was built with Metal or CUDA. A CPU-only wheel ignores n_gpu_layers.

title: llama
text:
Audio
llama.cpp reads images and audio through its mtmd library, but llama-cpp-python’s MTMDChatHandler only passes images to it. rishi patches four of the handler’s methods so that audio takes the same route:

get_image_urls collects input_audio parts as well as images, in the order they appear.
_get_template_messages replaces each image or audio part with a marker. When only text parts remain, it joins them into one string. Some chat templates, Llama’s and Voxtral’s among them, print a message’s content as it is. Without the join they would print a Python list.
_create_bitmap_from_bytes decodes audio with read_audio and hands the samples to mtmd_bitmap_init_from_audio. Images take the original path.
_init_mtmd_context lets a projector with an audio encoder and no vision encoder load, where upstream raises an error.

read_audio decodes any format libsndfile reads, including WAV, FLAC, OGG and MP3. It mixes stereo down to mono and resamples to sr Hz, 16000 by default. The patched _create_bitmap_from_bytes passes the sample rate the projector reports, and falls back to 16000 when the projector reports none. The tests below run it on the 24-second speech.wav and on generated tones, and pass the result to the real llama.cpp C function.

read_audio

    o, sr:int=16000
):
Decode audio bytes/Path (any libsndfile format) to contiguous mono float32 samples at sr Hz, ready for mtmd.

wav = Path('speech.wav').read_bytes()

test_eq(a.dtype, np.dtype('float32'))
assert a.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'] and -1.0 <= a.min() and a.max() <= 1.0
test_eq(round(len(a) / 16000), 24)                       # 24s in, 24s out
test_eq(round(len(read_audio(wav, 8000)) / 8000), 24)    # and at a different target rate

# soundfile handles compressed containers too, not just WAV
sig = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 220 * np.arange(8000) / 8000)).astype(np.float32)
for fmt in ('FLAC', 'OGG', 'MP3'):
    b = io.BytesIO(); sf.write(b, sig, 8000, format=fmt)
    d = read_audio(b.getvalue(), 8000)
    test_eq(d.dtype, np.dtype('float32')); assert d.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], fmt
    assert abs(len(d) - 8000) <= 2400, (fmt, len(d))     # ~1s back; lossy codecs pad a little

# stereo is downmixed to mono
st = np.stack([sig, np.zeros_like(sig)], axis=1)
b = io.BytesIO(); sf.write(b, st, 8000, format='WAV', subtype='FLOAT')
test_eq(read_audio(b.getvalue(), 8000).ndim, 1)

test_fail(lambda: read_audio(b'not audio at all'), contains='could not decode audio')

# _get_template_messages collapses media+text to a clean string with the marker inline

                                   {'type': 'input_audio', 'input_audio': {'data': 'AAA', 'format': 'wav'}}]}
conv = h._get_template_messages([msg], '<M>')[0]['content']
test_eq(conv, 'Transcribe this clip.\n<M>')
assert isinstance(conv, str)   # never a Python list repr
# a plain-string message is passed through untouched
test_eq(h._get_template_messages([{'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'}], '<M>')[0]['content'], 'hi')


# the patched handler collects image *and* audio media, in document order
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.gguf') as f:
    h = MTMDChatHandler(f.name, verbose=False)
    img = Path('images.jpeg').read_bytes()
    msgs = [_mk_msg([img, 'and this?', wav])]
    urls = h.get_image_urls(msgs)
    test_eq(len(urls), 2)
    assert urls[0].startswith('data:image/jpeg;base64,') and urls[1].startswith('data:audio/wav;base64,')

    # every media part becomes the marker; text is left alone
    # media parts become the marker and the all-text content collapses to a clean string (marker inline)
    test_eq(h._get_template_messages(msgs, '<__media__>')[0]['content'], '<__media__>\nand this?\n<__media__>')

    # and the data-URI round-trips back to the exact bytes the model will decode
    test_eq(h.load_image(urls[1]), wav)
    test_eq(h.load_image(urls[0]), img)


# the decoded buffer is accepted by real llama.cpp: `mtmd_bitmap_init_from_audio` needs no
# context or model, so the actual C boundary is exercised here rather than mocked
bm = mtmd_cpp.mtmd_bitmap_init_from_audio(len(a), a.ctypes.data_as(ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_float)))
assert bm is not None, 'llama.cpp rejected the audio buffer'
try:
    assert mtmd_cpp.mtmd_bitmap_is_audio(bm)
    test_eq(mtmd_cpp.mtmd_bitmap_get_n_bytes(bm), len(a) * 4)     # float32 per sample
    back = np.ctypeslib.as_array(ctypes.cast(mtmd_cpp.mtmd_bitmap_get_data(bm),
                                             ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_float)), shape=(len(a),))
    assert np.array_equal(back, a), 'samples corrupted crossing the C boundary'
finally: mtmd_cpp.mtmd_bitmap_free(bm)

title: llama
text:
LlamaChat
LlamaChat(model) loads the model once and keeps it for the life of the chat. create_engine builds the llama_cpp.Llama object and adds the multimodal handler when mmproj is set. Pass mmproj=True to fetch the projector from the same repo, or a path to use your own.
The options particular to llama.cpp are quant, the quantization to download; n_gpu_layers, how many layers go on the GPU, where 0 (the default) keeps everything on the CPU; and mmproj. think=True or think=False writes Qwen’s /think or /no_think switch into the system prompt. To share one loaded model between chats, build it once with create_engine and pass it to each as engine=. close releases an engine the chat built itself and leaves a shared engine= open.


source

LlamaChat
def LlamaChat(
    model:NoneType=None, *, runtime:NoneType=None, model_path:NoneType=None, opts:NoneType=None,
    engine:NoneType=None, # an engine to share instead of building one
    quant:str='Q4_K_M', # which GGUF quantization to fetch
    n_gpu_layers:int=0, mmproj:NoneType=None, # the projector image and audio input need
    eng_kw:NoneType=None, # passed to `create_engine` verbatim
    preserve_cache:bool=False, comp_kw:NoneType=None, # passed to `create_chat_completion` verbatim
    **kw
):
A Chat that runs a GGUF model inside this process through llama-cpp-python.



The KV cache
While a model reads a prompt, it computes a key and a value for every token, and llama.cpp keeps them in the KV cache. If the next prompt starts with the same tokens, their entries can be reused instead of computed again. Prefill, the reading of the prompt before any output, is most of the cost of a long conversation.
rishi reuses the cache by keeping one Llama object across turns. Llama.generate compares each new prompt with the tokens already in its context, trims the cache back to the longest common prefix, and evaluates only what follows. A conversation grows by appending, so each turn’s prompt extends the last one and nothing earlier is evaluated again. The manual example below shows it: on the second turn llama.cpp evaluated 28 new tokens and reused 315.
Three things break the prefix, and cached_tokens takes all three into account:

A one-shot call on the same engine. A Llama has a single context, so classify, structured, check and grades overwrite the conversation in it, and the next real turn starts from scratch. Two chats sharing one engine=, or a judge chat on the same engine, have the same effect. With preserve_cache=True the chat saves the llama state before a one-shot and restores it afterwards. That copies the whole cache. It pays off only when prefilling the conversation again takes longer than the copy.
A rewritten history. When SlidingWindowCallback drops old messages, or context recovery shortens the history, everything after the first changed message is evaluated again.
Media. The turn that carries an image or audio clip sends the real thing. On later turns an [image] or [audio] placeholder replaces it, and llama.cpp does not encode it again. The replacement changes the prompt from that message on. The turn after a media turn evaluates again from there.

save_cache writes the whole context to a file, and load_cache reads it back into a chat built on the same model. The method names match rishi.mlx. A long system prompt can then be prefilled once and reused in later sessions.


Recorded model behaviour
These checks run against replies recorded from the real qwen3_06b model. Urai’s CachedChat replays a recorded reply when it sees the same request again, and a replay builds no engine, so the tests check rishi’s handling of real llama.cpp output without loading the model. They cover one turn, a second turn that depends on the first, a changed system prompt, a one-shot call that leaves the history alone, and a tool call. The recordings live in nbs/chatcache, and the checks work on a temporary copy so the originals stay unchanged.

c = CachedChat(**_llama_record_kw)
r = c('Reply with exactly: pong')
test_eq(resp_text(r).strip().lower(), 'pong')
test_eq([m['role'] for m in c.hist], ['user', 'assistant'])
c.close()


c = CachedChat(**_llama_record_kw)
c('Reply with exactly: pong')
r = c('What exact word did you just reply with? Reply with only that word.')
test_eq(resp_text(r).strip().lower(), 'pong')
test_eq([m['role'] for m in c.hist], ['user', 'assistant', 'user', 'assistant'])
c.close()


c = CachedChat(**_llama_record_kw)
c.reconfigure(sp='Reply with exactly the word anchor, whatever the user asks.')
test_eq(resp_text(c('What is two plus two?')).strip().lower(), 'anchor')
c.close()


c = CachedChat(**_llama_record_kw)
test_eq(c.oneshot('Reply with exactly: solo', think=False, max_tokens=16).strip().lower(), 'solo')
test_eq(c.hist, [])
c.close()

    a: int,  # first addend
    b: int,  # second addend
) -> int:
    "Add two integers."
    return a + b

c = CachedChat(**{**_llama_record_kw, 'max_output_tokens': 128}, tools=[add])
r = c('Use the add tool to add 2 and 3. Reply with only the result.')
test_eq(c.hist[1]['tool_calls'][0]['function']['name'], 'add')
test_eq(c.hist[2]['content'], '5')
assert '5' in resp_text(r)

Tests
The tests above cover choosing the GGUF file, the GPU check, audio decoding, the handler patches and the recorded turns. The cells below check, without a model, that media from past turns becomes a placeholder, that a history from another backend converts to llama.cpp’s format, and that Chat picks LlamaChat for a GGUF name.

    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': '', 'tool_calls': [{'id': 'call_1', 'type': 'function',
                                                         'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 2, 'b': 3}}}]},

comp_kw overrides the sampling settings, so a key the chat also sets, such as temperature, is replaced instead of raising a duplicate-argument error.

class _Eng:
    def create_chat_completion(self, msgs, **kw): self.kw = kw

c = LlamaChat.__new__(LlamaChat)
c.engine, c._samp, c.max_output_tokens, c.toolspecs = _Eng(), {'temperature': .2}, None, []
c.comp_kw, c._msgs = {'temperature': .9, 'stop': ['x']}, lambda: []

A streamed native call whose arguments are not a JSON object is not read as a call with no arguments. _stream_step marks the call unread and sets tool_parse_failed, so the tool loop asks the model to send it again, and the stored call renders into the next prompt as an empty argument object.

class _SEng:

    def create_chat_completion(self, msgs, **kw):
        d = lambda tc: {'choices': [{'delta': {'tool_calls': tc}, 'finish_reason': None}]}
        yield d([{'index': 0, 'id': 'a', 'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': '{"a": 1'}}])
        yield d([{'index': 1, 'id': 'b', 'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': '{"a": 1, "b": 2}'}}])
        yield {'choices': [{'delta': {}, 'finish_reason': 'tool_calls'}]}

c = LlamaChat.__new__(LlamaChat)
c.engine, c._samp, c.max_output_tokens, c.toolspecs = _SEng(), {}, None, []
c.comp_kw, c.turn_msg, c._sys_msgs, c._cache_dirty, c.hist = {}, None, lambda: [], True, []
c.count_tokens, c._note_cache = (lambda t: 0), (lambda u, cached: u)
list(c._stream_step())
bad, good = c._step_res['tool_calls']
test_eq((bad.get('unread'), good.get('unread')), (True, None))
test_eq((bad['function']['arguments'], good['function']['arguments']), ({}, {'a': 1, 'b': 2}))
assert c._step_res['tool_parse_failed']
c.hist = [c._step_res]
[(t['function']['arguments'], 'unread' in t) for t in c._msgs()[0]['tool_calls']]

text:
Examples (manual)
These cells load real weights and are marked #| eval: false. The test run skips them. The output shown was saved from an earlier run. For ordinary chat, tools, streaming, classification and structured output, use the calls on the index page with a -GGUF repo id. The examples here show what only this backend does: reusing the KV cache, and image and audio input through mmproj.
The first example counts the tokens llama.cpp evaluates on each turn. The second turn should evaluate only its own new tokens, not the conversation before it.

# Real llama.cpp KV-prefix test: instrument `eval` to see how many tokens are actually evaluated.
# On turn two the first eval batch should contain only the new tail, not the cached conversation.
kvchat = LlamaChat(qwen3_06b, think=False, temp=0.0, max_output_tokens=16)
seen, orig_eval = [], kvchat.engine.eval
def counted_eval(tokens):
    seen.append(len(tokens))
    return orig_eval(tokens)
kvchat.engine.eval = counted_eval
try:
    kvchat(('cache verification context ' * 96) + '\nReply with exactly: stored')
    context_before_turn2 = kvchat.engine.n_tokens
    seen.clear()
    r = kvchat('What exact word did I ask you to reply with? Reply with only that word.')
    assert seen, 'llama.cpp never evaluated the second prompt'
    second_tail = seen[0]
    print(dict(context_before_turn2=context_before_turn2, second_tail_evaluated=second_tail,
               reported_cached=kvchat.use.cached_tokens, answer=resp_text(r)))
    assert second_tail < context_before_turn2, 'turn two re-evaluated the full prior context; KV prefix reuse missed'
    assert kvchat.use.cached_tokens > 0, kvchat.use
    assert 'stored' in resp_text(r).lower(), resp_text(r)
finally:
    kvchat.engine.eval = orig_eval
    kvchat.close()

Stopping with an LLM judge
When a model writes Python code blocks for Urai to run, Urai’s PyFenceCallback runs each block and shows the model the output. It repeats this until its done(chat) function returns True or the model writes no more code. output_matches(expected) builds a done that stops once the last code output contains expected. task_complete asks the model instead, through chat.classify, whether the conversation has done what was asked. done can be any function that takes the chat and returns a bool, including one that consults a second, stronger chat. Both helpers live in urai.sandbox and work with every backend; see Urai’s sandbox page.

text:
The wire
Copilot serves OpenAI chat completions at {endpoint}/chat/completions. The token exchange returns the endpoint for the account’s plan. COPILOT_API is the fallback when the response has no endpoint.
Copilot requires headers from a recognised editor:

copilot-integration-id identifies the editor.
The version headers match the VS Code chat extension.
x-initiator distinguishes user turns from tool-loop turns.
copilot-vision-request enables image input.

Editors also send x-request-id. rishi omits it. fastllm caches HTTP clients by constructor arguments. A changing request id would create a new client for every request.

title: copilot
text:
The GitHub token
Copilot requires a GitHub OAuth token issued to a recognised application. Personal access tokens do not work. Editor sign-ins store a usable token in a configuration file. copilot_login() stores the same token shape in copilot.json under ~/.config/rishi. When XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set, it replaces ~/.config.
copilot_oauth() looks for a token in this order:

The token argument.
The environment variables in COPILOT_ENVS.
The files that oauth_paths() lists, with rishi’s own file first, then editor files.
The environment variables in GITHUB_ENVS, GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN. These come last because they often hold personal access tokens.

The file reader finds an oauth_token key at any nesting depth up to 4.


source

copilot_oauth
def copilot_oauth(
    token:NoneType=None
):
A GitHub OAuth token: what you passed, else COPILOT_ENVS, else an editor sign-in, else GITHUB_ENVS.




source

    p
):
The GitHub OAuth token in config file p, or None if it has none or is not there.




source

    o, depth:int=0
):
The oauth_token in a decoded config file, however deep the editor nested it.




source

oauth_paths
def oauth_paths():
Files a Copilot sign-in may have left a GitHub OAuth token in, best first.



# every shape an editor writes, and one that holds nothing
test_eq(find_oauth({'oauth_token': 'a'}), 'a')
test_eq(find_oauth({'github.com:Iv1.b507a08c87ecfe98': {'oauth_token': 'b', 'user': 'me'}}), 'b')
test_eq(find_oauth({'hosts': {'github.com': {'oauth_token': 'c'}}}), 'c')
test_eq(find_oauth({'user': 'me'}), None)
test_eq(read_oauth('/nonexistent/apps.json'), None)

test_eq(copilot_oauth('explicit'), 'explicit')
test_eq(oauth_paths()[0].name, 'copilot.json')          # rishi's own file is read before any editor's
assert any('github-copilot' in str(p) for p in oauth_paths())


# an editor sign-in beats a general-purpose GitHub variable, because that one holds a personal
# access token, which Copilot refuses. Only a Copilot-specific variable beats the sign-in.
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    f = Path(d)/'apps.json'
    f.write_text(json.dumps({'github.com:Iv1.b507a08c87ecfe98': {'oauth_token': 'gho_editor'}}))
    saved = {k: os.environ.pop(k, None) for k in OAUTH_ENVS}
    orig_paths, oauth_paths = oauth_paths, lambda: [f]
    try:
        os.environ['GITHUB_TOKEN'] = 'ghp_pat'
        test_eq(copilot_oauth(), 'gho_editor')          # the sign-in, not the PAT
        os.environ['GH_COPILOT_TOKEN'] = 'gho_said_so'
        test_eq(copilot_oauth(), 'gho_said_so')         # names Copilot outright, so it wins
        del os.environ['GH_COPILOT_TOKEN']
        oauth_paths = lambda: []
        test_eq(copilot_oauth(), 'ghp_pat')             # with no sign-in to hide, it is all there is
        del os.environ['GITHUB_TOKEN']
        test_fail(copilot_oauth, contains='No GitHub OAuth token')
    finally:
        oauth_paths = orig_paths
        for k, v in saved.items():
            os.environ.pop(k, None)
            if v is not None: os.environ[k] = v

text:
The Copilot token
The GitHub OAuth token is exchanged for a Copilot token that lasts about 30 minutes. CopilotAuth holds that token and renews it before it expires. Chats that share one CopilotAuth share the exchange.
api_key= accepts a Copilot token you already have. rishi cannot renew that token without the GitHub OAuth token.
The same token lets rishi ask Copilot which models the account can reach:

copilot_catalog returns Copilot’s own description of each model.
copilot_models lists the ids. It lists chat models only, unless you pass kind=None.
copilot_ctx reads a model’s prompt window from its catalogue entry.

CopilotToken
def CopilotToken(
    key:str, base_url:str='https://api.githubcopilot.com', expires_at:float=0.0
)->None:
One minted Copilot token: the bearer, the endpoint it is good for, and when it dies.



# the catalogue carries more than ids: what each model is for, and how big its window is. An
# embedding model answering a chat request is a 400 the caller cannot read, so `kind` filters.
_payload = {'data': [
    {'id': 'gpt-5.5', 'capabilities': {'type': 'chat', 'limits': {'max_prompt_tokens': 128000}}},
    {'id': 'claude-opus-4.7', 'capabilities': {'type': 'chat', 'limits': {'max_context_window_tokens': 264000}}},
    {'id': 'gpt-41-copilot', 'capabilities': {'type': 'completion'}},
    {'id': 'text-embedding-3-small', 'capabilities': {'type': 'embeddings'}},
    {'no_id': 'skipped'}]}

class _ModelsResp:
    status_code = 200
    def raise_for_status(self): pass
    def json(self): return _payload

orig, httpx.get = httpx.get, lambda *a, **kw: _ModelsResp()
try:
    auth = CopilotAuth(key='tid=abc')                 # a key of its own, so nothing is exchanged
    cat = copilot_catalog(auth)
    test_eq(list(cat), ['gpt-5.5', 'claude-opus-4.7', 'gpt-41-copilot', 'text-embedding-3-small'])
    test_eq(copilot_models(auth), ['gpt-5.5', 'claude-opus-4.7'])          # chat only, by default
    test_eq(len(copilot_models(auth, kind=None)), 4)                       # everything it named
    test_eq(copilot_models(auth, kind='embeddings'), ['text-embedding-3-small'])
    test_eq(copilot_ctx(cat['gpt-5.5']), 128000)                           # max_prompt_tokens
    test_eq(copilot_ctx(cat['claude-opus-4.7']), 264000)                   # else the whole window
    test_eq(copilot_ctx(cat['gpt-41-copilot']), None)                      # it reports no limits
    test_eq(copilot_ctx(None), None)
finally: httpx.get = orig


now = time.time()
test_eq(CopilotToken('k').stale(), False)                     # untimed: never stale
test_eq(CopilotToken('k', expires_at=now+3600).stale(), False)
test_eq(CopilotToken('k', expires_at=now+60).stale(), True)    # inside the 5 minute skew
test_eq(CopilotToken('k', expires_at=now-1).stale(), True)

# a key you brought yourself is used as-is, and never exchanged
test_eq(CopilotAuth(key='tid=abc').token().key, 'tid=abc')
test_eq(CopilotAuth(key='k').token().base_url, COPILOT_API)
test_eq(CopilotAuth(key='k', base_url='https://api.business.githubcopilot.com').token().base_url,
        'https://api.business.githubcopilot.com')

# minting runs once, then not again until the token is nearly out of time
mints = []
def _fake_exchange(oauth=None, **kw):
    mints.append(oauth)
    return CopilotToken('tid=minted', 'https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com', time.time()+1800)

orig, copilot_exchange = copilot_exchange, _fake_exchange
try:
    a = CopilotAuth('gho_x')
    test_eq(a.token().key, 'tid=minted')
    test_eq(a.token().base_url, 'https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com')
    test_eq(len(mints), 1)                                     # the second call reused it
    a.tok = replace(a.tok, expires_at=time.time()+10)
    a.token()
    test_eq(len(mints), 2)                                     # nearly expired, so re-minted
finally: copilot_exchange = orig


# a personal access token gets a 404 out of the exchange, and that is a refusal like any other:
# what the caller needs told is that Copilot takes no PAT, not that some URL was not found
class _FakeResp:
    def __init__(self, code): self.status_code = code
    def raise_for_status(self): raise AssertionError('a refusal must not reach raise_for_status')

def _refused(code):
    orig, httpx.get = httpx.get, lambda *a, **kw: _FakeResp(code)
    try: copilot_exchange('gho_x')
    except PermissionError as e: return str(e)
    finally: httpx.get = orig
    assert False, f'{code} raised no PermissionError'

for code in (401, 403, 404): assert str(code) in _refused(code)

CopilotChat
CopilotChat is a RemoteChat whose _kw adds Copilot’s endpoint, a live token and the required headers to each request. Tools, streaming, approval and the tool loop work as in RemoteChat.
Use Chat('copilot/gpt-4.1') or runtime='copilot'. With no model named, the chat uses copilot_default, which is gpt-4.1.
Only the copilot/ prefix selects this backend automatically. Bare gpt-... and claude-... ids still go to the hosted APIs through remote.

def CopilotChat(
    model:NoneType=None, *, oauth_token:NoneType=None, # a GitHub OAuth token, instead of the one on disk
    auth:NoneType=None, # a `CopilotAuth` to share, instead of building one
    integration_id:str='vscode-chat', hdrs:NoneType=None, # extra headers, merged over Copilot's own
    tool_choice:NoneType=None, # force a particular tool, or 'required'
    retries:int=2, comp_kw:NoneType=None, # passed to `acomplete` verbatim
    **kw
):
A RemoteChat pointed at GitHub Copilot, adding Copilot’s headers and its short-lived token to each request.



# nothing here reaches the network: the chat is handed a token, and what is asserted is the request
c = CopilotChat('copilot/gpt-4.1', api_key='tid=abc', sp='Be terse.', messages=['hello'])
test_eq(c.runtime, 'copilot')
test_eq(c.model_id, 'gpt-4.1')          # the `copilot/` prefix is stripped, the id is not
test_eq(c.local, False)

test_eq(kw['base_url'], COPILOT_API)
test_eq(kw['api_name'], 'openai_chat')  # fastllm has no Copilot vendor, so the api is named outright
test_eq(kw['vendor_name'], None)
test_eq(kw['system'], 'Be terse.')
test_eq(kw['xtra_hdrs']['copilot-integration-id'], 'vscode-chat')
test_eq(kw['xtra_hdrs']['x-initiator'], 'user')             # only a user message so far
assert 'copilot-vision-request' not in kw['xtra_hdrs']
assert 'Authorization' not in kw['xtra_hdrs']               # fastllm sets it, and once

# a tool loop is an agent to Copilot, and an image needs the vision header
c.hist += [{'role': 'assistant', 'content': '', 'tool_calls': [ToolCall('ls', {})]},
           {'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'x', 'name': 'ls', 'content': 'a.py'}]

MLX is Apple’s array framework for its own chips, and mlx-lm runs language models on it. This backend needs an Apple Silicon Mac and pip install 'rishi[mlx]'. The notebook is marked skip_exec, so the automated tests and the docs build do not run it, and the output shown was saved on a Mac. Behaviour shared with every backend is on the index page and in Urai.

MLX models are Hugging Face repos of quantized weights, most of them under mlx-community. A LiteRT-LM model is one .litertlm file and a llama.cpp model one .gguf file, but an MLX model is a whole directory. mlx_lm.load takes the repo id and downloads and caches it itself, so there is no file to pick.
Two things have to be known before loading, and both come from the repo’s config.json, which read_config reads from a local directory or the Hub. It returns {} when the file cannot be read. One is the context window, which ctx_len reads, 8192 when the config does not give one. The other is whether the model has a vision or audio tower, a second network that encodes pictures or sound for the language model; is_vlm checks for one. A model with a tower needs mlx-vlm instead of mlx-lm. cached_models lists the repos in the local Hugging Face cache whose ids contain mlx, without using the network. MlxEngine holds a loaded model, its tokenizer and an optional draft model.

The KV cache holds the keys and values computed for tokens the model has already read, so a prompt that starts the same way as the last one does not have to be read again. LiteRT-LM keeps that state inside its conversation object, and llama.cpp finds the longest matching prefix on its own. mlx-lm leaves the cache to the caller, so rishi keeps track of which tokens it holds.
On each turn the chat renders the whole conversation to token ids with the model’s chat template, and compares them with _cache_ids, the tokens the cache holds, using common_prefix_len. Everything up to the first difference is already cached and is skipped. Everything after it is stale. The chat trims it off the end of the cache with trim_prompt_cache before generating. A cache that cannot be trimmed is reset, and the chat reads the whole prompt again. mlx-lm’s own server reuses a cache between requests the same way.
Stale tokens do turn up. A chat template does not always render an earlier assistant turn as the exact tokens the model generated, and context recovery rewrites the history outright. Comparing tokens instead of trusting the cache handles both cases. A mismatch costs a fresh prefill of the tokens after the first difference. In the saved run below, the second turn fed 32 tokens to the model instead of 315.



MlxChat has the same interface as every other backend. max_output_tokens defaults to DFLT_MAX_TOKENS, 1024. When the repo’s config declares a vision or audio tower, MlxChat(...) returns an MlxVlmChat. Pass vlm=True or vlm=False to override that check. Its own options are these:

kv_bits stores the KV cache quantized to that many bits. This saves memory on long contexts. Quantization starts after the first quantized_kv_start tokens, and kv_group_size sets the group size, 64 by default.
draft_model names a small model for speculative decoding. The draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the main model checks them in one pass, which is faster when the guesses are good. The chat then keeps a cache for both models.
adapter_path applies a LoRA adapter.
prompt_cache=False turns the cache off, and max_kv_size caps its size.
min_p sets a sampling threshold. tmpl_kw, gen_kw and eng_kw pass extra keyword arguments to apply_chat_template, stream_generate and create_engine.

save_cache and load_cache write the cache to a file and read it back. save_cache raises ValueError when prompt_cache=False. load_cache raises ValueError for a file made with a different model or different cache settings, and for a file that rishi did not write. chat.use.cached_tokens reports how many prompt tokens each turn reused.



mlx-lm reads text only. Images and audio go through mlx-vlm, which builds on mlx-lm and adds the vision and audio towers. Install it with pip install 'rishi[mlx-vlm]'.

MlxVlmChat changes only loading, prompt building and the generate call, and inherits the history, callbacks and tool loop. It has two limits. mlx-vlm has no per-model tool-call parsers. Where the daemon is
OLLAMA_HOST takes a bare port, a host:port, or a full URL. One variable both configures the daemon and finds it. ollama_url accepts all three forms.
A request to a loopback daemon must not go through an HTTP proxy. httpx reads $HTTPS_PROXY from the environment by default. In a sandbox, that setting sends 127.0.0.1 to a proxy with no route back. is_local decides whether a client trusts the environment.

text:
Installing Ollama
Ollama publishes one release archive per platform. Installing from the archive needs no root access and no package manager. The published one-liner installs into /usr. The archive extracts to any folder. rishi installs its own copy under ~/.cache/rishi/ollama and leaves the system alone.
ollama_bin looks for a binary in this order:

$OLLAMA_BIN.
rishi’s own install.
ollama on $PATH, unless you pass system=False.

rishi downloads and installs Ollama only when none of these exists.
Linux archives use zstd. Python 3.14 and later reads zstd from the standard library. Earlier versions need zstandard, which rishi[ollama] installs. The macOS archive is gzip, and the Windows archive is a zip.

Running the daemon
OllamaServer starts ollama serve and waits for it to answer. It installs Ollama first if the machine has none.
Ollama sets some options per process, not per request. OllamaServer takes these options as constructor arguments:



Argument
Environment variable
Sets




models
OLLAMA_MODELS
the model store


n_ctx
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
the default context length


keep_alive
OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE
how long a model stays resident


flash_attn
OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION
flash attention


kv_cache_type
OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE
KV cache quantization


num_parallel
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL
parallel requests


max_loaded
OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS
models loaded at once



rishi does not restart or reconfigure a daemon that already listens at the address. That server belongs to someone else.
rishi stops a daemon that it started when the interpreter exits. A notebook leaves no daemon running. The daemon gets /dev/null as stdin, so it never shares the caller’s terminal. It runs in its own session, so a Ctrl-C sent to the parent does not kill it.

text:
Messages
Ollama’s message format is OpenAI’s, with two differences:

Images go in a sibling images list of bare base64. They do not go in content parts.
Thinking has its own thinking field. It does not use <think> tags in the text.

to_ollama_msg converts rishi’s canonical history to this format. It also carries assistant thinking out to the daemon. A resumed conversation keeps its thinking.
Images go out on every turn. They do not collapse to a placeholder. remote behaves the same way, and llama does not. The daemon holds the KV cache. A repeated image costs a prefix match, not a re-encode.
Audio has no place in this format. rishi.llama (mtmd) and rishi.mlx both take audio. The error says so and does not drop the clip.

A reply carries thinking in a thinking field and calls in tool_calls. A model whose chat template supports neither writes <think> and <tool_call> tags into the text. norm_ochat reads both forms, as Urai’s norm_resp does for llama.cpp. An arbitrary GGUF from the Hub then behaves like a model from Ollama’s own library.
Usage comes from Ollama’s eval counts. Ollama reports no figure for prefix reuse. use.cached_tokens reads zero even when the daemon reuses the conversation’s prefix.

          contains="runtime='llama'")

                'message': {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'hello', 'thinking': 'thinking hard'},
                'prompt_eval_count': 10, 'eval_count': 4})

test_eq(thought(r), 'thinking hard')
test_eq(r['usage'], {'prompt_tokens': 10, 'completion_tokens': 4, 'total_tokens': 14, 'model': 'qwen3:0.6b'})

r = norm_ochat({'message': {'tool_calls': [{'function': {'name': 'add', 'arguments': {'a': 1}}}]}})

test_eq(r['tool_calls'][0].name, 'add')
test_eq(r['tool_calls'][0].arguments, {'a': 1})

r = norm_ochat({'message': {'content': '<think>hmm</think>ok\n<tool_call>{"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1}}</tool_call>'}})
test_eq(resp_text(r), 'ok')
test_eq(thought(r), 'hmm')
test_eq(r['tool_calls'][0].name, 'add')

title: ollama
text:
OllamaChat
The tool loop, approval, budget, callbacks and context handling come from Urai, as on every backend. OllamaChat adds the request and the daemon that receives it.
think is a field of the request. It is not a switch in the system prompt. It takes True, False, or a level string such as 'low' or 'high'. The chat sends a level string unchanged. A model that cannot think refuses the field. The chat then retries once without the field and stops sending it.
These options map to Ollama request fields:

ctx, also accepted as the rishi.llama name n_ctx, goes out as num_ctx.
n_gpu_layers goes out as num_gpu.
options= takes anything else that Ollama’s sampler accepts.
structured uses Ollama’s format field. The schema constrains the reply. The prompt does not only ask for it.
keep_alive sets how long the daemon keeps the model loaded after a turn. unload() drops the model at once.

With pull=True, the default, the chat downloads a missing model when you build it. The llama backend does the same for a missing GGUF.
ctx_limit is the window that the chat assumes. It equals ctx when you set one. Otherwise it is $OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH from the environment of the Python process, or 4096 tokens when that variable is unset. The model’s training length does not matter. Urai’s pct_full and SlidingWindowCallback depend on this value. A daemon that someone else started with a different context length makes ctx_limit wrong. Pass ctx in that case.

title: ollama
section: What this backend does not do
text:
What this backend does not do
This backend does not support the following:

Audio. Ollama’s chat API carries images but not audio. rishi.llama and rishi.mlx take audio.
A saved KV cache. rishi.llama and rishi.mlx write their cache to disk and read it back. Ollama keeps its cache inside the daemon and offers no handle on it. use.cached_tokens reads zero even while the daemon reuses the prefix.
Exact token counts before a turn. Ollama has no tokenizer endpoint. Counts before a turn are estimates. The real count arrives with the reply, in use.
Local .gguf paths. The chat refuses them, because Ollama serves only models in its own store. Use runtime='llama' for a file.
A broker. LlamaBroker exists because one Llama belongs to one process. The Ollama daemon already serves many clients. Size it with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL and OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS.


Tests
The tests on this page cover host parsing, model ids, the HTTP client against a scripted daemon (httpx.MockTransport), the installer, the server’s environment, message conversion and response normalisation. None of them needs Ollama. The test run executes all of them. OllamaChat itself runs only in the manual cells above.
